Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding

Ziyi Guan ††thanks: MIT. ziyiguan@mit.edu.    Yael Tauman Kalai ††thanks: MIT. tauman@mit.edu.    Ron Rothblum ††thanks: Succinct. rothblum@gmail.com    Zoe Xi ††thanks: MIT. zoexi@mit.edu.
Abstract

Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost.

In this work, we introduce rewindable interactive proofs (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model’s state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography.

In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.

RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover’s machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

    1. A.1 Relation to RIPs

1 Introduction

As AI capabilities grow rapidly, a critical problem is: how can we ensure that AI systems remain safe and behave as intended? One major concern is that, as we are training AI models to perform increasingly complex tasks, we may no longer be able to efficiently verify the accuracy of their outputs. As a result, we may not be able to verify that they are behaving in a way that aligns with our intentions. This problem of providing accurate training supervision for increasingly powerful AI models is known as scalable oversight.

Verifiable computation has been studied for decades in cryptography and computational complexity. This research has led to proof systems that allow a powerful but untrusted “prover” (in our setting, a powerful AI model) to convince a weak “verifier” (a weaker AI model or a human) that the output of a hard computation is correct [12, 41, 7, 6, 45, 59, 15, 57].

In this work, we observe that scalable oversight has some unique characteristics that make existing approaches either inapplicable or less efficient than they could be. First, the prover is not an external party but rather an AI model whose execution the verifier controls. In particular, the verifier can rewind the model to an earlier state and continue the interaction without the model remembering what happened in previous runs. To capitalize on this, we consider a new proof-system model which we call rewindable interactive proofs (RIPs),11 1 Not to be confused with another RIP. Our provers are merely rewound, never harmed. in which the verifier is allowed to rewind the prover in this way. This model is closely related to previous proof-systems studied in the literature such as MIPs [12] and PCPs [41, 7, 6], but we show that it can have significant efficiency gains over them.

Second, classical results in proof systems do not apply directly to our setting, because the computations we wish to verify may involve functions that we can’t see the inner workings of—such a function can be used to represent human judgment or query access to an external database, for example. We model such “black-box” functions as oracles, and say that a proof system relativizes if its guarantees hold with respect to any oracle. Relativization is believed to be essential for AI safety purposes, because we do not know what sorts of capabilities AI may have in the future. The UK AISI team even writes that “in order to be relevant to AI safety, an interactive proof result must relativize” [52]. The difficulty is that classical results in proof systems, including the celebrated 𝖨𝖯=𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{IP}=\mathsf{PSPACE} and 𝖬𝖨𝖯=𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯\mathsf{MIP}=\mathsf{NEXP} theorems, do not relativize [28], and moreover results show that efficient verification is impossible for arbitrary oracle-aided computations [43, 42, 49, 44, 35, 10].

For a concrete example of where scalable oversight is needed, consider the scenario of training an LLM to determine which laws a company has violated based on hundreds of pages of records. The LLM outputs one bit for each law (representing yes or no), and now we need to verify whether these bits are correct or not. The straightforward way of doing this would be to have a human expert carefully read through the documents, but this seems unreasonably expensive, especially to produce just one training label. In a scenario like this, we would like to have a more efficient training protocol, especially one that is more efficient in its use of human judgments. As another example, we may consider a scenario where we train an LLM to answer questions using a large public dataset, such as the web; we would like to be able to verify that an output of this LLM is correct efficiently, making few queries to the dataset.

Various approaches to scalable oversight have been proposed in the literature [37, 55, 51], including some based on relativizing proof systems. One prominent example of such an approach is debate, which was introduced by Irving, Christiano, and Amodei [51]. In an AI debate, there are two powerful AI models, or provers, who claim different outputs, and the provers debate each other to try to convince a verifier that their output is the correct one. The verifier is extremely efficient, or succinct, meaning that it runs in much less time and makes far fewer oracle queries than it would need to run the computation on its own. The authors show that 𝖣𝖤𝖡𝖠𝖳𝖤\mathsf{DEBATE}, the class of problems which admit a debate protocol, is powerful: in the language of computational complexity theory, 𝖣𝖤𝖡𝖠𝖳𝖤=𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{DEBATE}=\mathsf{PSPACE} (where 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE} is the class of problems solvable in polynomial space). Moreover, this result relativizes.

However, debate makes the strong assumption that one of the provers is truthful, i.e., one of the AI models is guaranteed to argue for the correct answer. Intuitively, this means that the verifier has one of the powerful AI models on his side. But scalable oversight is especially important precisely when we do not know whether we can trust any AI model. Recently, Chen, Kalai, and Xi [30] sought to remove this assumption by constructing “doubly-efficient” interactive proofs [45]. In an interactive proof [46, 9], a prover interacts with a verifier to convince him of a claim; a doubly-efficient one has an efficient prover as well as an efficient verifier. Since this is impossible for arbitrary oracle computations, [30] instead give protocols for a natural restricted setting where the computation is robust, meaning that the output does not change even if a small fraction of answers to oracle queries are modified. However, these protocols still require substantially more work from the verifier than debate. A natural question, then, is:

Can we obtain a more efficient relativizing interactive proof without assuming any prover is truthful?

Motivated by this question, we give a positive answer for robust oracle computations in the RIP model: by exploiting the verifier’s ability to rewind the prover, we obtain strong efficiency guarantees without assuming that any prover is truthful.

1.1 Our results

We introduce and formally define rewindable interactive proofs, and construct a relativizing RIP for robust oracle-aided computations, with a succinct verifier and a linear-time prover. We also implement our protocol and evaluate its performance experimentally.

The model.

In an interactive proof, a prover and a verifier exchange messages, after which the verifier accepts or rejects. The proof must be complete, meaning that the honest prover convinces the verifier of a correct output, and sound, meaning that no cheating prover can convince it of an incorrect output, except with small probability. An RIP is an interactive proof in which the verifier has one extra power: at any point, it may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there, as one would restore an AI model from a save point (Section 5.1 gives the formal definition). Completeness is as usual: the honest prover must convince the verifier, now across whatever rewinds the verifier performs. Soundness, on the other hand, asks less than it does of a standard proof system. A standard proof system must be sound against every cheating prover, however it behaves; an RIP need only be sound against provers that the verifier can rewind, whose answer after a rewind cannot depend on anything the verifier did after the restored state. This is a weaker guarantee, and it is what makes the model powerful: the verifier can question the prover about one state as many times as it likes, and the prover never learns the other questions. We emphasize that soundness violated if a cheating prover has access to external storage that is not rewound.

A relativizing RIP for robust computations.

Following Chen, Kalai, and Xi [30], we model the computation as an oracle Boolean circuit and call it ε\varepsilon-robust if its output does not change when up to an ε\varepsilon fraction of the oracle’s answers are modified. Our main result is a relativizing RIP for verifying the output of any robust oracle circuit, with a succinct verifier and a prover that runs in linear time.

Theorem 1.1 (Informal; see Theorem 5.8).

Let COC^{O} be an oracle circuit with nn input bits, mm output bits, and SS gates, whose oracle queries have polylogarithmic length. After a one-time preprocessing step taking O~​(n+m+S)\widetilde{O}(n+m+S) time, there is a relativizing RIP for verifying the output of COC^{O} on any input with respect to which it is ε\varepsilon-robust, with the following guarantees:

  • •

    The honest prover always convinces the verifier of a correct output, while a cheating prover (even a computationally unbounded one) can convince the verifier of an incorrect output with probability at most 1/31/3.

  • •

    The verifier runs in O~​(n+m+1/ε)\widetilde{O}(n+m+1/\varepsilon) time and makes O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon) oracle queries.

  • •

    The honest prover runs in O⁡(n+m+S)+O~​(1/ε)O(n+m+S)+\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon) time.

  • •

    The number of rounds is O⁡(log⁡(n+m+S))O(\log(n+m+S)) and the total communication is O~​(1/ε)\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon).

Here O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot) hides factors polylogarithmic in n+m+Sn+m+S, and running times count field operations.

In the preprocessing step, the verifier reads the description of the circuit and stores a representation of it, which it reuses in every evaluation of the circuit; the cost is thus amortized over all evaluations, which suits our setting, where a fixed circuit is evaluated on many inputs. Some such step is necessary to achieve online verification time sublinear in the size of a general circuit, and preprocessing is standard in efficient proof systems [34, 60, 29]; see Remark 3.22.

Comparison with [30] and debate.

Compared with the protocols of [30], after the preprocessing step our verifier’s running time depends only on the lengths of the input and output and on the robustness parameter, instead of on the size or depth of the circuit, and its number of oracle queries depends only on the robustness parameter; compared with their succinct protocol, ours is statistically sound, uses no cryptography, and has a linear-time rather than a polynomial-time prover. Unlike debate, our protocol does not assume that a prover is truthful.

Why not concretely efficient SNARGs?

The proof systems deployed in practice, notably in blockchains [14, 63], are SNARGs, succinct non-interactive arguments. Why not take one off the shelf? First, off-the-shelf SNARGs do not handle oracle-aided computations, even robust ones. Second, their soundness rests on unproven cryptographic assumptions, from standard ones such as collision-resistant hash functions to more aggressive ones chosen for concrete efficiency. As AI brings such assumptions under increasing scrutiny (recent AI-discovered results, still under review, claim to refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis [56, 38] and, assuming them, give a subexponential algorithm for the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem [2]), it is unclear whether this is a prudent tradeoff for scalable oversight. RIPs address both concerns: they handle robust oracle-aided computations without cryptographic assumptions and are sound even against computationally unbounded provers. Perhaps surprisingly, dispensing with cryptography can also improve prover efficiency: rewinding avoids the cost of cryptographic commitments (Remark 5.9), and our second experiment demonstrates the resulting speedup.

Experiments.

We complement our theoretical result by implementing the protocol and running two experiments. The first is a proof-of-concept experiment inspired by the MNIST debate experiment of Irving, Christiano, and Amodei [51]: we run the protocol once, at soundness error 2−402^{-40}, on robust oracle circuits with between 282^{8} and 2262^{26} oracle gates, whose oracle is the debate experiment’s judge, a sparse MNIST classifier. Across this range the verifier makes a median of about 7676 oracle queries, against up to 2262^{26} needed to evaluate the largest circuit directly, and its online running time falls below that of direct evaluation from about seven million oracle gates on, to an eighth of it at the largest size.

For our second experiment, we consider Flock [27], a state-of-the-art SNARG built from an interactive oracle proof (IOP) [15, 57] (see Section 2) for batch evaluation of the BLAKE3 hash function. To study the efficiency gains of rewinding, we compile Flock’s IOP into an RIP and find that its prover runs 1.81.8 to 2.1×2.1\times faster than Flock’s own SNARG prover (Section 6.3).

1.2 Related work

Relativizing proof systems.

Relativization has been studied extensively as a barrier in computational complexity theory, and notably the classical results on interactive proofs, e.g., the celebrated 𝖨𝖯=𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{IP}=\mathsf{PSPACE} and 𝖬𝖨𝖯=𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯\mathsf{MIP}=\mathsf{NEXP} theorems, do not relativize [28]. Additionally on the negative side, results show that efficient verification is impossible for arbitrary oracle-aided computations (even when the security guarantee is relaxed to hold only against efficient dishonest provers) [43, 42, 49, 44, 35, 10]. Our work circumvents these barriers by restricting to the setting of robust oracle computation. On the positive side, prior work has shown that 𝖨𝖯=𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{IP}=\mathsf{PSPACE} and 𝖬𝖨𝖯=𝖭𝖤𝖷𝖯\mathsf{MIP}=\mathsf{NEXP} do algebrize, meaning that they relativize if the proof system is also given a low-degree extension of the oracle [1], and there has also been work on constructing relativizing succinct cryptographic proof systems in some structured oracle models [36, 32, 31, 33, 30].

Interactive proofs for scalable oversight.

There has been a recent line of work studying interactive proofs as an approach to scalable oversight, starting with a paper by Irving, Christiano, and Amodei on “AI safety via debate” [51]. Their model assumes that the debating provers are computationally unbounded; later, Brown-Cohen, Irving, and Piliouras introduced doubly-efficient debate, where the provers are guaranteed to be efficient [22]. More recent works on debate have focused on its limitations, e.g, the “obfuscated arguments problem,” where a lying debating prover can make it very hard for the other prover to find the flaw in her argument [11, 23, 24]. Very recently, Chen, Kalai, and Xi initiated the study of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight without a truthful prover, constructing protocols with a succinct verifier and a polynomial-time prover for certain classes of oracle computations [30]. Our work considers the setting of robust computation that they introduce; we leverage rewinding to improve the efficiency of their protocols.

Interactive proofs for trustworthy machine learning.

There is also a line of work on applying interactive proofs to problems of trust in machine learning [4, 5, 48, 54, 64]. In particular, Amit, Goldwasser, Paradise, and Rothblum [4] introduce self-proving models, which are trained to provide both an answer and an interactive proof that the answer is correct; their focus is on training models to produce proofs for computations that already admit interactive proofs, whereas we construct new interactive proofs for oracle-aided computation.

2 Technical Overview

Here, let us briefly outline the key ideas behind our construction.

We model the computation that the verifier wishes to verify as an oracle Boolean circuit COC^{O}, i.e., a Boolean circuit that may contain gates that make calls to an arbitrary oracle O:{0,1}∗→{0,1}O:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}. We assume that the oracle circuit is ε\varepsilon-robust with respect to the verifier’s input, meaning that its output on this input does not change if at most an ε\varepsilon-fraction of answers to its oracle queries are changed (see Definition 3.14 for a formal definition). Given an oracle circuit COC^{O}, an input xx for which COC^{O} is ε\varepsilon-robust, a claimed output aa, and access to OO, the prover and the verifier engage in a rewindable interactive proof (RIP, Section 5) that CO​(x)=aC^{O}(x)=a. Recall that the verifier may rewind the prover to any earlier state of the interaction and continue from there.

Our goal is to design a protocol that is efficient enough to use in practice. Most practical proof systems are built from an interactive oracle proof (IOP) [15, 57], which is an interactive proof where the prover sends long messages but the verifier reads only a few bits of each message, because IOPs admit very efficient provers and verifiers. We first construct a relativizing IOP and then turn it into a relativizing RIP that inherits the IOP’s efficiency.

A relativizing IOP (Section 4).

To start, a natural strategy is to try to turn the oracle circuit COC^{O} into a circuit without oracle gates and then use standard IOPs. To “deoraclize” the circuit, suppose that the prover provides a string ww containing a claimed answer for each oracle gate. We can then define a circuit CwC_{w} without oracle gates, which is COC^{O} except with each oracle gate replaced by the corresponding answer in ww. The basic idea is to have the prover send the string ww in the first round of the IOP and then prove that Cw​(x)=aC_{w}(x)=a. Then the verifier can check that the answers in ww are correct with respect to OO.

The verifier cannot check that all the answers in ww are correct, since this would require making all the oracle calls needed in order to run the computation, which he cannot afford. But the verifier does not actually need to do this, since we assume COC^{O} is ε\varepsilon-robust: if CO​(x)≠aC^{O}(x)\neq a, then any ww satisfying Cw​(x)=aC_{w}(x)=a must contain more than an ε\varepsilon-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, so the verifier can catch an incorrect oracle answer with good probability by sampling O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon) answers in ww.

To obtain stronger efficiency guarantees, instead of ww itself, we have the prover send an encoding of a witness consisting of ww together with a “transcript” of evaluating CwC_{w} on xx. The prover and verifier then run an IOP to check that this encoding is close to the encoding of a valid witness for Cw​(x)=aC_{w}(x)=a. The advantage of using an encoding is that the verifier can later recover a few bits of this same witness, with the prover’s help, without reading the entire witness. In particular, the verifier can sample a few oracle gates, recover the claimed answer in ww for each oracle gate and the corresponding query using the transcript, and check that the pair is correct using OO. To achieve this, we construct a variant of an IOP that we call an encoded-witness IOP (Section 3.4).

Relativizing IOP →\rightarrow relativizing RIP (Section 5.2).

Now we turn our relativizing IOP into a relativizing RIP. The idea is similar to the one behind the standard proof for turning a (non-relativizing) IOP into an MIP [15] (see Appendix A for MIPs and their relation to RIPs). We have the RIP verifier simulate the IOP verifier and the RIP prover simulate the IOP prover, except that the “IOP” prover computes her long messages but does not send them. If the verifier simply asked the prover for the bits he wants to read, she could answer adaptively, e.g., her answer to the verifier’s second query to some message could depend on his first query. Instead, whenever the verifier wants to read a bit in some message, he rewinds the prover to her state right after she computed that message and asks her for the bit. Her answer then cannot depend on his other queries, so she cannot do better than an IOP prover who fixes each message before the verifier queries it, and the soundness error is that of the IOP. Rewinding thus allows the RIP to be as efficient as the IOP.

Experiments (Section 6).

We implement our protocol and run two experiments. The first evaluates it on robust oracle circuits and measures what the verifier saves over evaluating the circuit directly. The second compares it with an existing proof system. Since no relativizing protocol has an implementation, we compare with a state-of-the-art proof system for an oracle-free computation, which is built from an IOP: compiling the same IOP into an RIP instead measures what rewinding saves.

The first experiment is a proof of concept inspired by the MNIST debate experiment of Irving, Christiano, and Amodei [51]. We use a sparse MNIST classifier, which predicts a digit from six revealed nonzero pixels of an MNIST image, to define our oracle. Given a “sparse view” of an MNIST image and a candidate digit, the oracle outputs whether the classifier predicts that digit. Our circuits query this oracle on many random sparse views of an image and output whether a majority of the views vote for the candidate digit.

We run the protocol once, at soundness error 2−402^{-40}, on 50 MNIST test images while increasing the number qCq_{C} of oracle gates from 282^{8} to 2262^{26}. The robustness parameter remains nearly constant across these circuit sizes, and the median number of oracle queries made by the verifier stays between 7474 and 8080. At the largest circuit size, the verifier makes 840,000×840{,}000\times fewer oracle queries than are needed to evaluate the circuit directly. The verifier’s online running time is also sublinear in the circuit size, growing substantially more slowly than direct evaluation: it falls below direct evaluation at about seven million oracle gates, and at qC=226q_{C}=2^{26} is 0.12×0.12\times the time required to evaluate the circuit directly. The prover, which also generates the witness, takes about 60×60\times the time of direct evaluation at the largest sizes.

For the second experiment we use Flock [27], a proof system for batch evaluation of an ordinary Boolean circuit with no oracle gates, namely the BLAKE3 hash function. Flock is built from an IOP, which is not by itself a realistic proof system, since the prover sends long strings; Flock compiles it into a SNARG using cryptography. We compile the same IOP into an RIP instead, which saves the cryptographic compilation: the prover no longer commits to its proof strings, and since a cheating prover gets one attempt per execution rather than unlimited offline retries, the IOP can run at a lower security level and over a smaller field. On instances of size 2222^{22} to 2342^{34}, our prover runs 1.81.8 to 2.1×2.1\times faster than Flock’s prover (Section 6.3).

3 Preliminaries

Here we introduce some definitions and tools that we use.

Definition 3.1 (Language).

A language ℒ⊆{0,1}∗\mathcal{L}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*} is a set of binary strings. We think of a language as a decision problem: given an instance 𝕩∈{0,1}∗\mathbbm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*}, we want to determine whether 𝕩∈ℒ\mathbbm{x}\in\mathcal{L}.

Definition 3.2 (Relation).

A relation R⊆{0,1}∗×{0,1}∗R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*}\times\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*} is a set of pairs (𝕩,𝕨)(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w}), where 𝕩\mathbbm{x} is an instance and 𝕨\mathbbm{w} is a witness for 𝕩\mathbbm{x}. The language associated with RR is ℒ≔{𝕩:∃𝕨⁡(𝕩,𝕨)∈R}.\mathcal{L}\coloneq\{\mathbbm{x}:\exists\mathbbm{w}(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R\}.

Definition 3.3 (Oracle and oracle access).

An oracle is a fixed function O:{0,1}∗→{0,1}O:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}; in particular, its answer to a query does not depend on earlier queries. We write that an algorithm has oracle access to OO if it can send a query 𝗊𝗋𝗒∈{0,1}∗\mathsf{qry}\in\{0,1\}^{*} and receive the answer string O⁡(𝗊𝗋𝗒)O(\mathsf{qry}) in one timestep.

Definition 3.4 (Relativized language).

For an oracle OO, a relativized language ℒO\mathcal{L}^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is a language whose membership may depend on OO.

Definition 3.5 (Relativized relation).

For an oracle OO, a relativized relation ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is a relation whose membership may depend on OO. Its associated relativized language is ℒRO\mathcal{L}_{R^{O}}.

Definition 3.6 (Equality polynomial).

Let 𝔽\mathbb{F} be a finite field and h≥0h\geq 0 an integer. The equality polynomial 𝖾𝗊:𝔽h×𝔽h→𝔽\mathsf{eq}:\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}\times\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}\to\mathbb{F} is

𝖾𝗊⁡(r,e)≔∏i=1h(ri​ei+(1−ri)​(1−ei)).\mathsf{eq}(r,e)\coloneq\prod_{\scriptscriptstyle i=1}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}\bigl(r_{\scriptscriptstyle i}e_{\scriptscriptstyle i}+(1-r_{\scriptscriptstyle i})(1-e_{\scriptscriptstyle i})\bigr).

For b,e∈{0,1}hb,e\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}, 𝖾𝗊⁡(b,e)\mathsf{eq}(b,e) is 11 if b=eb=e and 00 otherwise.

Definition 3.7 (Multilinear extension).

Let 𝔽\mathbb{F} be a finite field and h≥0h\geq 0 an integer. We interpret every vector v∈𝔽2hv\in\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle 2^{\scriptscriptstyle h}} as a function v:{0,1}h→𝔽v:\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}\to\mathbb{F}. The multilinear extension of vv is the unique polynomial v^:𝔽h→𝔽\widehat{v}:\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}\to\mathbb{F} of degree at most one in each variable satisfying v^​(b)=v​(b)\widehat{v}(b)=v(b) for every b∈{0,1}hb\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}. Explicitly,

v^​(r)=∑b∈{0,1}hv⁡(b)​𝖾𝗊​(r,b),\widehat{v}(r)=\sum_{\scriptscriptstyle b\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle h}}v(b)\,\mathsf{eq}(r,b),

where 𝖾𝗊\mathsf{eq} is the equality polynomial (Definition 3.6). For a binary string of length 2h2^{\scriptscriptstyle h}, we view its bits as elements of 𝔽\mathbb{F} and use the same definition. For a vector or string of any other length, the multilinear extension is that of its zero-padding to the next power-of-two length 2h2^{\scriptscriptstyle h}.

3.1 Oracle-aided computation and robustness

Following [30], we model the computation that the verifier verifies as an oracle Boolean circuit. Informally, this is a diagram that shows how to obtain an output string from an input string by applying some sequence of OR (∨\lor), AND (∧\land), and NOT (¬\neg) operations together with calls to an oracle. More formally, we have:

Definition 3.8 (Boolean circuit).

An nn-bit input, mm-bit output Boolean circuit is a directed acyclic graph with nn input vertices and an ordered list of mm output vertices. Input vertices have no incoming edges; every other vertex is a gate labeled ∨\lor or ∧\land with two incoming edges, or ¬\neg with one. Any vertex may be an output. A circuit CC is given by its description ⟨C⟩\langle C\rangle, a binary string that lists its gates in a fixed order, each with its label and its incoming edges, followed by the list of output vertices; we refer to gates by their position in this list.

On input x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n}, the value of the iith input vertex is the iith bit of xx, and each gate applies its operation to the values of its children, i.e., the vertices with edges going into the gate. The output of the circuit on xx consists of the values of the output vertices read in order. The size of a circuit is its number of gates.

Definition 3.9 (Oracle Boolean circuit).

For an oracle O:{0,1}∗→{0,1}O:\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*}\to\{0,1\}, an oracle Boolean circuit COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is a Boolean circuit that may also contain oracle gates. Each oracle gate has an arbitrary number of incoming edges. We view the input to an oracle gate as the string given by the values of its children read in order. The value of an oracle gate is OO applied to its input string.

Definition 3.10 (Family of circuits).

A family of circuits {Cn}n∈ℕ\{C_{\scriptscriptstyle n}\}_{\scriptscriptstyle n\in\mathbb{N}} consists of one circuit CnC_{\scriptscriptstyle n} with an nn-bit input and an m⁡(n)m(n)-bit output for each nn. It computes a function f:{0,1}∗→{0,1}∗f:\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*}\to\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*} if Cn​(x)=f​(x)C_{\scriptscriptstyle n}(x)=f(x) for every nn and every x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n}.

Definition 3.11.

Let COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} be an oracle circuit of size SS. We define the computation transcript on input xx to be the string that lists the values of all the gates in CC when run on input xx in order (using OO to evaluate oracle gates), and denote the computation transcript by

z=TrCO⁡(x)∈{0,1}S.z=\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}}(x)\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle S}.
Definition 3.12.

Suppose COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} has 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} oracle gates, and consider running CC on an input xx. We use

𝒬CO​(x)=𝒬=((𝗊𝗋𝗒1,𝖺𝗇𝗌1),…,(𝗊𝗋𝗒𝗊C,𝖺𝗇𝗌𝗊C))\mathcal{Q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}}(x)=\mathcal{Q}=((\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\mathsf{ans}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}),\ldots,(\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}},\mathsf{ans}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}}))

for the string of queries and answers that COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} makes to OO on input xx, where 𝗊𝗋𝗒i\mathsf{qry}_{i} (resp. 𝖺𝗇𝗌i\mathsf{ans}_{i}) is the input to (resp. output of) oracle gate ii. Call 𝒬\mathcal{Q} a query-answer trace. We write 𝒬in\mathcal{Q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{in}} (resp. 𝒬out\mathcal{Q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{out}}) for the string of queries (resp. answers) in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Definition 3.13 (De-oraclized circuit).

Let COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} be an oracle circuit with an input of length nn and 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} oracle gates. We say that its de-oraclized circuit is the (non-oracle) circuit CC with input (x,w)∈{0,1}n×{0,1}𝗊C(x,w)\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n}\times\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}} obtained by replacing, for every j∈[𝗊C]j\in[\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}], oracle gate jj with an input vertex with value wjw_{\scriptscriptstyle j}.

We next define robustness. Informally, the output of a robust oracle circuit should not change if at most a small fraction of answers to its oracle queries are incorrect. More formally, we define robustness as follows, adapting the definition that Chen, Kalai, and Xi use [30]:

Definition 3.14 (Robustness).

Let COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} be an oracle circuit with an input of length nn and 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} oracle gates, and let CC be its de-oraclized circuit (Definition 3.13). For an input (x,w)(x,w), where x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n} and w∈{0,1}𝗊Cw\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}}, and an index j∈[𝗊C]j\in[\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}], let 𝗊𝗋𝗒j​(w)\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle j}(w) denote the input to oracle gate jj in COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} when we run COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} on xx except with the value of each oracle gate replaced with the corresponding bit in ww. For ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1], we say that COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is 𝛆\varepsilon-robust with respect to x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n} if, for every w∈{0,1}𝗊Cw\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}} satisfying

|{j∈[𝗊C]:wj≠O⁡(𝗊𝗋𝗒j​(w))}|≤ε​𝗊C,\bigl|\{j\in[\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}]:w_{\scriptscriptstyle j}\neq O(\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle j}(w))\}\bigr|\leq\varepsilon\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C},

we have that C​(x,w)=CO​(x)C(x,w)=C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x).

Definition 3.15 (Circuit-satisfiability relation).

The circuit-satisfiability relation R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}} is the relation defined as follows. The instance is a triple 𝕩=(⟨C⟩,x,a)\mathbbm{x}=(\langle C\rangle,x,a), where ⟨C⟩\langle C\rangle is the description of a Boolean circuit with n+nwn+n_{\scriptscriptstyle w} input vertices, of which the first nn form the public input and the remaining nwn_{\scriptscriptstyle w} the private input, an output of length mm, and SS gates, x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n} is a public input, and a∈{0,1}ma\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle m} is a claimed output. The witness is a pair 𝕨=(w,z)∈{0,1}nw×{0,1}S\mathbbm{w}=(w,z)\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n_{\scriptscriptstyle w}}\times\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle S} of a private input and a transcript. Then

(𝕩,𝕨)∈R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳⟺z=TrC(x,w)∧C(x,w)=a,(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}(x,w)\;\land\;C(x,w)=a,

where TrC\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} is the computation transcript of Definition 3.11.

Definition 3.16 (Oracle-circuit-evaluation relation).

Fix an oracle OO. The oracle-circuit-evaluation relation R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is the relativized relation (Definition 3.5) defined as follows. The instance is a triple 𝕩=(⟨CO⟩,x,a)\mathbbm{x}=(\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle,x,a), where ⟨CO⟩\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle is the description of an oracle circuit with an input of length nn, output of length mm, and SS gates, x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle n} is an input, and a∈{0,1}ma\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle m} is a claimed output. The witness is a transcript z∈{0,1}Sz\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle S}. Then

(𝕩,z)∈R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫O⟺z=TrCO(x)∧CO(x)=a,(\mathbbm{x},z)\in R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}}(x)\;\land\;C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)=a,

where TrCO\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}} is the computation transcript of Definition 3.11.

Remark 3.17 (Transcript as witness).

The witness of Definition 3.15 is a private input ww together with the entire transcript zz, and the witness of Definition 3.16 is the entire transcript. The transcript is not needed to define either relation, as it is determined by the instance and ww in Definition 3.15 and by the instance alone in Definition 3.16. Including it nevertheless allows succinct verification, since the verifier can check an encoding of the witness at a few positions instead of evaluating the circuit (Definitions 3.32, 3.36 and 4.1).

3.2 Interactive oracle proofs

An interactive oracle proof (IOP), introduced in [15, 57], lets a powerful prover convince a weak verifier that an instance has a valid witness by sending long proof strings that the verifier checks at a few locations. The parties may interact over several rounds.

Definition 3.18 (Interactive oracle proof).

An interactive oracle proof for a relation RR is an interactive protocol between a probabilistic polynomial-time verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V} and a possibly computationally unbounded prover 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The parties receive a common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, and the honest prover additionally receives a witness 𝕨\mathbbm{w} with (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R.

In round ii, the prover sends a proof string πi\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle i} over a finite alphabet Σ\Sigma, which is a finite field in our constructions. The verifier has oracle access (Definition 3.3) to every proof string sent so far.

The protocol satisfies the completeness and soundness properties defined below.

We write ⟨𝒫​(𝕨),𝒱⟩​(𝕩)=1\langle\mathcal{P}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1 when the verifier accepts after interacting with the prover on common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x}. Note that we denote the IOP prover and verifier by 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒱\mathcal{V}, rather than by 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐕\mathbf{V} as for rewindable interactive proofs (Section 5) and MIPs (Appendix A), to distinguish between the settings. The probabilities below are over the verifier’s private random bits (we assume without loss of generality that the prover is deterministic).

Definition 3.19 (Completeness).

An IOP for RR has perfect completeness if, for every (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R, the honest prover satisfies

Pr[⟨𝒫(𝕨),𝒱⟩(𝕩)=1]=1.\mathrm{Pr}\left[\langle\mathcal{P}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]=1.
Definition 3.20 (Soundness).

An IOP for RR has soundness error ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}} if, for every 𝕩∉ℒ\mathbbm{x}\notin\mathcal{L} and every possibly computationally unbounded cheating prover 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}},

Pr[⟨𝒫~,𝒱⟩(𝕩)=1]≤ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯(|𝕩|).\mathrm{Pr}\left[\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{P}},\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}(|\mathbbm{x}|).
Definition 3.21 (Relativizing IOP).

Fix an oracle OO and a relativizing relation ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O}. A relativizing IOP for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is an IOP for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} in which the verifier and prover, including a cheating prover, have black-box access to the same oracle OO. The protocol relativizes if its completeness, soundness, and efficiency guarantees hold for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} for every oracle OO.

Remark 3.22 (Preprocessing).

An instance may have the form 𝕩=(𝕩pre,𝕩post)\mathbbm{x}=(\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}},\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}), where 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} is long and is the same for many instances. In our setting 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} is the description of a circuit and 𝕩post\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} is an input together with a claimed output (Definition 3.16). An IOP with preprocessing has a verifier that is a pair 𝒱=(𝒱pre,𝒱post)\mathcal{V}=(\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}},\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}). First 𝒱pre\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} receives 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} and outputs a state 𝗌𝗍𝒱\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{V}}. Then 𝒱post\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} receives 𝗌𝗍𝒱\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{V}} and 𝕩post\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} and interacts with the prover. The verifier reads 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} only in the preprocessing, which is done once and whose state is reused for every 𝕩post\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}. Completeness and soundness are as in Definitions 3.19 and 3.20.

For the verifier’s online time to be sublinear in the size of a general circuit, we need to preprocess the circuit. Intuitively, without preprocessing the verifier must read the entire circuit, since two circuits that differ in one gate can produce different outputs on the same input. Preprocessing is standard in deployed proof systems [34, 60, 29]. Since we typically fix a circuit and evaluate it on many inputs, the one-time cost of preprocessing is amortized over all the evaluations. Preprocessing is unnecessary, however, for a circuit with a short description, since the verifier can then work from the description instead of reading the whole circuit [45, 39, 62, 65]. It is also unnecessary when a circuit is evaluated on a batch of inputs, since the verifier can read the circuit once per batch [27].

We track the following worst-case efficiency parameters of a (relativizing preprocessing) IOP:

  • •

    Proof length ℓ\ell: the total number of alphabet symbols in the proof strings.

  • •

    Proof query complexity 𝗊π\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\pi}: the total number of verifier queries to the proof strings.

  • •

    Round complexity 𝗋𝖨𝖮𝖯\mathsf{r}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{IOP}}: the number of back-and-forth rounds between the verifier and the prover. Queries to proof strings do not count as interaction rounds.

  • •

    Verifier oracle query complexity 𝗊O\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle O}: the number of verifier calls to the oracle OO, when present. These calls are counted separately from proof queries.

  • •

    Verifier preprocessing time t𝒱pret_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}}}: for an IOP with preprocessing (Remark 3.22), the running time of 𝒱pre\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}}, which bounds |𝗌𝗍𝒱||\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{V}}|.

  • •

    Verifier online time t𝒱t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{V}}: the running time of 𝒱post\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}, with random access to 𝗌𝗍𝒱\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{V}}.

  • •

    Prover running time t𝒫t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{P}}: the honest prover’s total running time.

3.3 Error-correcting codes

An error-correcting code maps a message to a longer string, its codeword, so that any two codewords differ in many positions. A locally decodable code [53] lets a decoder recover any symbol of the message from a few queries to a (possibly corrupted) codeword, and a relaxed locally decodable code [16] also allows the decoder to refuse to answer.

Definition 3.23 (Distance).

Let Σ\Sigma be a finite alphabet and ℓ\ell a positive integer. The distance Δ⁡(π,π′)\Delta(\pi,\pi^{\prime}) between π,π′∈Σℓ\pi,\pi^{\prime}\in\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} is the fraction of positions in which they differ. The distance between π\pi and a set S⊆ΣℓS\subseteq\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} is

Δ⁡(π,S)≔minπ′∈S⁡Δ⁡(π,π′),\Delta(\pi,S)\coloneq\min_{\scriptscriptstyle\pi^{\prime}\in S}\Delta(\pi,\pi^{\prime}),

and Δ⁡(π,S)≔1\Delta(\pi,S)\coloneq 1 if SS is empty. For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), we say that π\pi is 𝛅\delta-close to SS if Δ⁡(π,S)≤δ\Delta(\pi,S)\leq\delta, and 𝛅\delta-far from SS otherwise.

Definition 3.24 (Code).

Let Σ\Sigma be a finite alphabet and ℓ\ell a positive integer. A code is a set 𝒞⊆Σℓ\mathcal{C}\subseteq\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell}, whose elements are called codewords. Its relative distance is the minimum distance (Definition 3.23) between two distinct codewords,

Δ⁡(𝒞)≔minc≠c′∈𝒞⁡Δ⁡(c,c′).\Delta(\mathcal{C})\coloneq\min_{\scriptscriptstyle c\neq c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}\Delta(c,c^{\prime}).

For a finite alphabet Γ\Gamma and an integer k≥0k\geq 0, an encoding is an injective map 𝖤𝗇𝖼:Γk→Σℓ\mathsf{Enc}:\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k}\to\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell}. Its image is a code, and the relative distance of 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} is that of its image.

We write ℐ=(i1,…,i|ℐ|)∈[k]∗\mathcal{I}=(i_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,i_{\scriptscriptstyle|\mathcal{I}|})\in[k]^{\scriptscriptstyle*} for a list of positions and 𝕨|ℐ≔(𝕨i1,…,𝕨i|ℐ|)\mathbbm{w}|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}}\coloneq(\mathbbm{w}_{\scriptscriptstyle i_{1}},\ldots,\mathbbm{w}_{\scriptscriptstyle i_{|\mathcal{I}|}}) for the symbols of 𝕨∈Γk\mathbbm{w}\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k} at these positions.

Definition 3.25 (Relaxed local decoder).

Let 𝖤𝗇𝖼:Γk→Σℓ\mathsf{Enc}:\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k}\to\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} be an encoding. A relaxed local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} with query complexity 𝗊dec\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}} is a probabilistic algorithm 𝖣𝖾𝖼\mathsf{Dec} that receives a list ℐ\mathcal{I} of positions, has oracle access to a string c∈Σℓc\in\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell}, reads at most 𝗊dec\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}} symbols of cc, and outputs ζ∈Γ|ℐ|∪{⊥}\zeta\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle|\mathcal{I}|}\cup\{\bot\}. We write ζ←𝖣𝖾𝖼c​(ℐ)\zeta\leftarrow\mathsf{Dec}^{\scriptscriptstyle c}(\mathcal{I}) for its output.

Definition 3.26 (Completeness).

A relaxed local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} has perfect completeness if, for every 𝕨∈Γk\mathbbm{w}\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k} and every list ℐ\mathcal{I} of positions,

Pr⁡[ζ=𝕨|ℐ|ζ←𝖣𝖾𝖼𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)​(ℐ)]=1.\mathrm{Pr}\left[\zeta=\mathbbm{w}|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}}\;\middle|\;\zeta\leftarrow\mathsf{Dec}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w})}(\mathcal{I})\right]=1.
Definition 3.27 (Decoding error).

A relaxed local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} has decoding error ϵdec:(0,1)×ℕ→[0,1]\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{dec}}}:(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}\to[0,1] if, for every proximity parameter δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), every list ℐ\mathcal{I} of positions, every 𝕨∈Γk\mathbbm{w}\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k}, and every c~∈Σℓ\widetilde{c}\in\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} that is δ\delta-close to 𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w}) (Definition 3.23),

Pr⁡[ζ∉{𝕨|ℐ,⊥}|ζ←𝖣𝖾𝖼c~​(ℐ)]≤ϵdec​(δ,|ℐ|).\mathrm{Pr}\left[\zeta\notin\{\mathbbm{w}|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}},\bot\}\;\middle|\;\zeta\leftarrow\mathsf{Dec}^{\scriptscriptstyle\widetilde{c}}(\mathcal{I})\right]\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{dec}}}(\delta,|\mathcal{I}|).

In this paper we use a more relaxed notion, interactive local decoding, in which a prover helps the decoder. This relaxation is what enables efficient proving and verification: the encoding of Lemma 3.31 has linear length, and decoding a few positions costs the prover linear time and the decoder polylogarithmic time in the message length.

Definition 3.28 (Interactive local decoder).

Let Γ⊇{0,1}\Gamma\supseteq\{0,1\} be a finite alphabet and let 𝖤𝗇𝖼:Γk→Σℓ\mathsf{Enc}:\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k}\to\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} be an encoding (Definition 3.24). An interactive local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} is an interactive protocol between a probabilistic polynomial-time decoder 𝐃\mathbf{D} and a possibly computationally unbounded prover 𝒫dec\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}}. The parties receive a common input ℐ\mathcal{I}, a list of positions. The decoder has oracle access to a string π∈Σℓ\pi\in\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell}, and the honest prover receives 𝕨∈Γk\mathbbm{w}\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k} with π=𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)\pi=\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w}). The prover sends proof strings as in an IOP (Definition 3.18), and at the end the decoder outputs ζ∈Γ|ℐ|∪{⊥}\zeta\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle|\mathcal{I}|}\cup\{\bot\}.

We write ζ←⟨𝒫dec​(𝕨),𝐃π⟩​(ℐ)\zeta\leftarrow\langle\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathbf{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle\pi}\rangle(\mathcal{I}) for the output of the decoder. We track the efficiency parameters of an interactive local decoder as for an IOP (Section 3.2), with the queries to π\pi counted as proof queries.

Definition 3.29 (Completeness).

An interactive local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} has perfect completeness if, for every 𝕨∈Γk\mathbbm{w}\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k} and every list ℐ\mathcal{I} of positions, the honest prover satisfies

Pr⁡[ζ=𝕨|ℐ|ζ←⟨𝒫dec​(𝕨),𝐃𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)⟩​(ℐ)]=1.\mathrm{Pr}\left[\zeta=\mathbbm{w}|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}}\;\middle|\;\zeta\leftarrow\langle\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathbf{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w})}\rangle(\mathcal{I})\right]=1.
Definition 3.30 (Decoding error).

An interactive local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} has decoding error ϵdec:(0,1)×ℕ→[0,1]\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{dec}}}:(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}\to[0,1] if, for every proximity parameter δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), every list ℐ\mathcal{I} of positions, every 𝕨∈Γk\mathbbm{w}\in\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k}, every π~∈Σℓ\widetilde{\pi}\in\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} that is δ\delta-close to 𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w}) (Definition 3.23), and every possibly computationally unbounded cheating prover 𝒫~dec\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},

Pr⁡[ζ∉{𝕨|ℐ,⊥}|ζ←⟨𝒫~dec,𝐃π~⟩​(ℐ)]≤ϵdec​(δ,|ℐ|).\mathrm{Pr}\left[\zeta\notin\{\mathbbm{w}|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}},\bot\}\;\middle|\;\zeta\leftarrow\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},\mathbf{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle\widetilde{\pi}}\rangle(\mathcal{I})\right]\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{dec}}}(\delta,|\mathcal{I}|).
Lemma 3.31 ([25, 61]).

Let k≥1k\geq 1. There is a prime field 𝔽\mathbb{F} of size at least a sufficiently large polynomial in kk and at most polynomial in kk, and an injective encoding 𝖤𝗇𝖼:𝔽k→𝔽ℓ\mathsf{Enc}:\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle k}\to\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} with ℓ=O⁡(k)\ell=O(k), computable in O⁡(k)O(k) field operations, with relative distance at least a constant δ𝖤𝗇𝖼>0\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}}>0, such that for every constant proximity parameter δ∈(0,δ𝖤𝗇𝖼/4)\delta\in(0,\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}}/4) there is an interactive local decoder for 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} that, on a list ℐ\mathcal{I} of positions, has the following parameters, where the constants in the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) depend on δ\delta.

  • •

    Perfect completeness.

  • •

    Decoding error: ϵdec​(δ,|ℐ|)≤1/12\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{dec}}}(\delta,|\mathcal{I}|)\leq 1/12.

  • •

    Round complexity: O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k).

  • •

    Proof query complexity: O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k).

  • •

    Proof length: O⁡(k)O(k).

  • •

    Prover time: O⁡(k+|ℐ|)O(k+|\mathcal{I}|).

  • •

    Verifier time: O⁡((|ℐ|+1)​log⁡k)O((|\mathcal{I}|+1)\log k).

The decoder’s verifier has oracle access to a string of length k1/2+o⁡(1)k^{\scriptscriptstyle 1/2+o(1)} that depends only on kk and is computable in that time; in Lemma 3.36 the verifier computes it in its preprocessing.

Proof sketch.

𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} is the encoding of TensorSwitch [25], a tensor code of two linear-time encodable codes of constant rate and constant relative distance [61], so it has linear length, constant relative distance, and linear encoding time. TensorSwitch binds a string to a message by decoding its columns and then its rows, each within the unique decoding radius of the respective code; a string that is δ\delta-close to 𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w}) with δ<δ𝖤𝗇𝖼/4\delta<\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}}/4 has few enough undecodable columns for this to recover 𝕨\mathbbm{w}, and in this regime the hypotheses of TensorSwitch on the codes hold for every linear code. The decoder works as follows. The prover sends the claimed values ζ′∈𝔽|ℐ|\zeta^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle|\mathcal{I}|} of the positions in ℐ\mathcal{I}. The decoder picks a random r∈𝔽|ℐ|r\in\mathbb{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle|\mathcal{I}|}, and the parties run a sumcheck for the claim ∑iui​𝕨i=∑krk​ζk′\sum_{i}u_{\scriptscriptstyle i}\mathbbm{w}_{\scriptscriptstyle i}=\sum_{k}r_{\scriptscriptstyle k}\zeta^{\prime}_{\scriptscriptstyle k}, where u≔∑krk​eiku\coloneq\sum_{k}r_{\scriptscriptstyle k}e_{\scriptscriptstyle i_{k}} has |ℐ||\mathcal{I}| nonzero entries. This reduces the claim to one evaluation of the multilinear extension of 𝕨\mathbbm{w} at a random point, which the parties check against π\pi by running the remaining rounds of TensorSwitch’s commitment phase and its opening protocol. The decoder outputs ζ′\zeta^{\prime} if every check passes and ⊥\bot otherwise. If some ζk′≠𝕨ik\zeta^{\prime}_{\scriptscriptstyle k}\neq\mathbbm{w}_{\scriptscriptstyle i_{k}}, the combined claim is false except with probability 1/|𝔽|1/|\mathbb{F}| over rr, and then the sumcheck or the opening rejects except with error polynomially small in |𝔽||\mathbb{F}| plus the error of the opening, which is 2−λ2^{\scriptscriptstyle-\lambda} for O⁡(λ)O(\lambda) queries; λ=4\lambda=4 gives decoding error below 1/121/12. The prover runs the sumcheck in O⁡(k)O(k) field operations, since uu is sparse, and the opening in O⁡(k)O(k). The verifier runs in O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k) for the sumcheck, O⁡(|ℐ|​log⁡k)O(|\mathcal{I}|\log k) to evaluate the multilinear extension of uu at the random point, and O⁡(log⁡k)O(\log k) for the opening, which reads a preprocessed string of length k1/2+o⁡(1)k^{\scriptscriptstyle 1/2+o(1)} that depends only on the code. ∎

3.4 Encoded-witness IOPs

Here we define the notion of encoded-witness IOPs, which serve as a building block in our relativizing IOP in Section 4. An encoded-witness IOP is an IOP in which the prover’s first message is an encoding of its witness. Soundness is stated in terms of this first message [15, 13]. In addition, the encoding is required to have an interactive local decoder (Definition 3.28).

Definition 3.32 (Encoded-witness IOP).

Let RR be a relation whose witnesses are strings 𝕨∈{0,1}k\mathbbm{w}\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle k}, and let 𝖤𝗇𝖼:Γk→Σℓ\mathsf{Enc}:\Gamma^{\scriptscriptstyle k}\to\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell} be an encoding (Definition 3.24). An encoded-witness IOP for RR with encoding 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} is an IOP with preprocessing (𝒫,𝒱)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{V}) for RR (Definitions 3.18 and 3.22) in which the prover’s first message is a proof string π1∈Σℓ\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}\in\Sigma^{\scriptscriptstyle\ell}, and the honest prover sends π1≔𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨)\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}\coloneq\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w}), where the encoding 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} has an interactive local decoder (𝒫dec,𝐃)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},\mathbf{D}) (Definition 3.28). We write

(π1,b)←⟨𝒫⁡(𝕨),𝒱⟩​(𝕩)(\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},b)\leftarrow\langle\mathcal{P}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})

where π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} denotes the first message of the prover and bb denotes the decision bit of the verifier. The decoder has the completeness and decoding error of Definitions 3.29 and 3.30; the IOP has the completeness and soundness properties defined below.

Definition 3.33 (Completeness).

An encoded-witness IOP has perfect completeness if, for every (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R, the honest prover satisfies

Pr⁡[b=1|(π1,b)←⟨𝒫⁡(𝕨),𝒱⟩​(𝕩)]=1.\mathrm{Pr}\left[b=1\;\middle|\;(\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},b)\leftarrow\langle\mathcal{P}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})\right]=1.
Definition 3.34 (Soundness).

For an instance 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, let 𝒞𝕩≔{𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕨):(𝕩,𝕨)∈R}\mathcal{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbbm{x}}\coloneq\{\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbbm{w}):(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R\} be the set of encodings of valid witnesses. An encoded-witness IOP has soundness error ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯:(0,1)→[0,1]\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}:(0,1)\to[0,1] if, for every proximity parameter δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), every instance 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, and every possibly computationally unbounded cheating prover 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}},

Pr⁡[b=1∧Δ⁡(π1,𝒞𝕩)>δ|(π1,b)←⟨𝒫~,𝒱⟩​(𝕩)]≤ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯​(δ).\mathrm{Pr}\left[b=1\;\land\;\Delta\bigl(\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\mathcal{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbbm{x}}\bigr)>\delta\;\middle|\;(\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},b)\leftarrow\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{P}},\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})\right]\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}(\delta).
Remark 3.35 (Holographic proofs).

Encoded-witness IOPs are similar to holographic PCPs [8], PCPs of proximity [16], and IOPs of proximity [15, 57], in which the verifier has oracle access to an input and certifies that it is close to a language; here the input is the prover’s first message and the language is the set of encodings of valid witnesses. However, these proof systems only guarantee proximity to such an encoding, whereas we also need to recover positions of the witness from the first message, which is what the interactive local decoder provides.

Lemma 3.36 (Encoded-witness IOP for circuits, adapted from [29, 34, 26, 25]).

Consider instances of R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}} (Definition 3.15) whose circuit has a public input of length nn, a private input of length nwn_{\scriptscriptstyle w}, output length mm, and SS gates. Let N′≔S+n+nw+mN^{\prime}\coloneq S+n+n_{\scriptscriptstyle w}+m, and let 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} be the encoding with an interactive local decoder given by Lemma 3.31 for k≔N′k\coloneq N^{\prime}, applied to the witness (w,z)(w,z) padded with zeros to length N′N^{\prime}. Then, for every constant proximity parameter δ∈(0,δ𝖤𝗇𝖼/4)\delta\in(0,\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}}/4), with δ𝖤𝗇𝖼\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}} as in Lemma 3.31, R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}} has an encoded-witness IOP (𝒫ew,𝒱ew)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}},\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}}) with encoding 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} with the following parameters, where O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot) hides factors polylogarithmic in N′N^{\prime} and the constants in the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) depend on δ\delta.

  • •

    Perfect completeness.

  • •

    Soundness error: ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯​(δ)≤1/12\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}(\delta)\leq 1/12.

  • •

    Round complexity: O⁡(log⁡N′)O(\log N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Proof query complexity: O⁡(log⁡N′)O(\log N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Proof length: O⁡(N′)O(N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Prover time: O⁡(N′)O(N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Verifier preprocessing time: O~​(N′)\widetilde{O}(N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Verifier online time: O~​(n+m)\widetilde{O}(n+m).

Proof sketch.

The IOP is the standard compilation of a polynomial IOP into an IOP [34, 26], applied to the polynomial IOP for circuit satisfiability of HyperPlonk [29], with polynomials sent as codewords of the encoding 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} of Lemma 3.31 and evaluation claims checked by the proximity test of TensorSwitch [25]. The prover’s first message is 𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(w,z)\mathsf{Enc}(w,z), the encoding of the witness. The verifier’s preprocessing encodes the polynomials that describe the circuit and computes the string of Lemma 3.31, which is its O~​(N′)\widetilde{O}(N^{\prime}) cost; its online work is that of the polynomial IOP’s verifier, which reads only the public input and output, plus a polylogarithmic number of queries. Whenever the polynomial IOP’s verifier queries a polynomial at a point, the prover answers with the evaluation, and the two run the proximity test on the encoding and the claimed evaluation. For soundness, since δ\delta is below the unique decoding radius, every queried string is δ\delta-close to at most one codeword, and the proximity test ensures, except with its error, that every answer is an evaluation of the polynomial that this codeword encodes. The soundness of the polynomial IOP then applies to the polynomial encoded by the first message, so if the verifier accepts with probability above 1/121/12, the first message is δ\delta-close to the encoding of a valid witness. The prover runs in O⁡(N′)O(N^{\prime}) field operations, since the prover of HyperPlonk, the encoding, and the prover of the proximity test all do. The constants in the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) depend on δ\delta through the proximity test’s query complexity. ∎

4 Relativizing Interactive Oracle Proofs

In this section we construct a relativizing IOP (Definition 3.21) for the oracle-circuit-evaluation relation R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O} of Definition 3.16, that is, for proving that CO​(x)=aC^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)=a.

Theorem 4.1 (Relativizing IOP for robust oracle circuits).

Fix an oracle O:{0,1}∗→{0,1}O:\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*}\to\{0,1\} and 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1. Let COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} be an oracle circuit with an input of length nn, an output of length mm, and SS gates, and let N′≔S+n+mN^{\prime}\coloneq S+n+m. Suppose that the oracle queries of COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} have length polylogarithmic in N′N^{\prime}. Then R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O}, for instances (⟨CO⟩,x,a)(\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle,x,a) with this circuit such that COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is ε\varepsilon-robust with respect to xx, has a relativizing IOP with preprocessing (Remark 3.22) over a prime field of size polynomial in N′N^{\prime} with the following properties, where O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot) hides factors polylogarithmic in N′N^{\prime}, running times count field operations, and proof lengths count field elements.

  • •

    Perfect completeness.

  • •

    Soundness error: at most 1/31/3.

  • •

    Round complexity: O⁡(log⁡N′)O(\log N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Proof query complexity: O⁡(log⁡N′)O(\log N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Verifier oracle queries: O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon).

  • •

    Proof length: O⁡(N′)O(N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Prover time: O⁡(N′)+O~​(1/ε)O(N^{\prime})+\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon).

  • •

    Verifier preprocessing time: O~​(N′)\widetilde{O}(N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Verifier online time: O~​(n+m+1/ε)\widetilde{O}(n+m+1/\varepsilon).

Recall that we want a relativizing IOP for R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O}, that is, for the claim that CO​(x)=aC^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)=a, in which the verifier makes only a few queries to OO. Without oracle gates this would be ordinary circuit satisfiability, which standard IOPs handle; the difficulty is the oracle gates, which the verifier cannot evaluate itself without making 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} oracle queries. Intuitively, we can ask the prover to supply the answer to every oracle query. This turns COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} into its de-oraclized circuit (Definition 3.13), an ordinary circuit whose evaluation an IOP can verify, and leaves the verifier with the task of checking that the supplied answers agree with OO. Checking all of them would again take 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} oracle queries, but by robustness a wrong output can only be reached by lying about more than an ε\varepsilon fraction of the answers, so a few random spot checks suffice. Concretely, the construction combines the encoded-witness IOP for circuits of Lemma 3.36 with random sampling of oracle gates. The prover encodes the evaluation of the de-oraclized circuit of COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} (Definition 3.13) on input xx and the oracle answers in its transcript, and proves that the de-oraclized circuit outputs aa. The verifier then samples a few oracle gates, decodes the query and the recorded answer at each of them from the encoded witness, and checks that each answer agrees with the oracle. By robustness (Definition 3.14), a wrong output forces more than an ε\varepsilon fraction of the recorded answers to be wrong, so O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon) samples suffice. Section 4.1 gives the protocol and Section 4.2 proves the theorem.

4.1 Construction

We describe the protocol (𝒫,𝒱)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{V}) for R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O}. Fix OO, ε\varepsilon, and a field 𝔽\mathbb{F} as in Theorem 4.1, an instance 𝕩=(⟨CO⟩,x,a)\mathbbm{x}=(\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle,x,a) with 𝕩pre=⟨CO⟩\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}}=\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle and 𝕩post=(x,a)\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}=(x,a), and the witness z=TrCO⁡(x)z=\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}}(x). Let CC be the de-oraclized circuit of COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} (Definition 3.13), let w∈{0,1}𝗊Cw\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}} be the values of zz at the oracle gates, and let

u≔w∥TrC⁡(x,w),u\coloneq w\mathbin{\|}\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}(x,w),

be the witness of R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}} (Definition 3.15) for the instance (⟨C⟩,x,a)(\langle C\rangle,x,a). The answer at oracle gate jj is the bit wjw_{\scriptscriptstyle j} of uu, and each bit of its query is a bit of xx or of uu, at a position determined by ⟨CO⟩\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle. Let (𝒫ew,𝒱ew)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}},\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}}) be the encoded-witness IOP of Lemma 3.36 for a constant proximity parameter δ∈(0,δ𝖤𝗇𝖼/4)\delta\in(0,\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}}/4), let 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} be its encoding, and let (𝒫dec,𝐃)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},\mathbf{D}) be the interactive local decoder of 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} for proximity parameter δ\delta (Lemma 3.31). The protocol is as follows.

  1. 1.

    IOP: 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒱\mathcal{V} run (𝒫ew,𝒱ew)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}},\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}}) on (⟨C⟩,x,a)(\langle C\rangle,x,a) with witness uu. This gives the first message π1=𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(u)\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}=\mathsf{Enc}(u) and the decision bit bb.

  2. 2.

    Decoding: 𝒱\mathcal{V} samples a uniformly random set {j1,…,jt}\{j_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,j_{\scriptscriptstyle t}\} of t≔min⁡{𝗊C,⌈(ln⁡6)/ε⌉}t\coloneq\min\{\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C},\lceil(\ln 6)/\varepsilon\rceil\} oracle gates and lets ℐ\mathcal{I} be the positions of their answers and query bits. Then 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒱\mathcal{V} run (𝒫dec,𝐃)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},\mathbf{D}) on π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} and ℐ\mathcal{I}, which gives ζ∈{0,1}|ℐ|∪{⊥}\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle|\mathcal{I}|}\cup\{\bot\}. Unless ζ=⊥\zeta=\bot, this yields for each k∈[t]k\in[t] a decoded answer 𝖺𝗇𝗌~k\widetilde{\mathsf{ans}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k} at the jkj_{\scriptscriptstyle k}-th oracle gate and, together with the bits of xx, a decoded query 𝗊𝗋𝗒~k\widetilde{\mathsf{qry}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k}.

  3. 3.

    Decision: 𝒱\mathcal{V} accepts if and only if b=1b=1, ζ≠⊥\zeta\neq\bot, and O⁡(𝗊𝗋𝗒~k)=𝖺𝗇𝗌~kO(\widetilde{\mathsf{qry}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k})=\widetilde{\mathsf{ans}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k} for every k∈[t]k\in[t].

4.2 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Completeness.

Suppose that CO​(x)=aC^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)=a. Then ww holds the answers of OO in the evaluation of COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} on xx, so C⁡(x,w)=aC(x,w)=a and (w,TrC⁡(x,w))(w,\operatorname{Tr}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}(x,w)) is a valid witness. Hence b=1b=1 with probability 11 by the completeness of the encoded-witness IOP, and ζ=u|ℐ\zeta=u|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}} with probability 11 by the completeness of the decoder (Lemma 3.31). The decoded bits are bits of uu, so 𝗊𝗋𝗒~k\widetilde{\mathsf{qry}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k} is the query at the jkj_{\scriptscriptstyle k}-th oracle gate and 𝖺𝗇𝗌~k=O⁡(𝗊𝗋𝗒~k)\widetilde{\mathsf{ans}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k}=O(\widetilde{\mathsf{qry}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k}).

Soundness.

Consider an instance 𝕩=(⟨CO⟩,x,a)\mathbbm{x}=(\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle,x,a) with CO​(x)≠aC^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)\neq a, and let 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}} be a cheating prover for our IOP. Since δ<δ𝖤𝗇𝖼/4\delta<\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}}/4 and 𝖤𝗇𝖼\mathsf{Enc} has relative distance at least δ𝖤𝗇𝖼\delta_{\mathsf{Enc}} (Lemma 3.31), the first message π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} of 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}} is δ\delta-close to the encoding of at most one string. Let (w∗,z∗)(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*}) be this string if it is a valid witness of R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}} for (⟨C⟩,x,a)(\langle C\rangle,x,a), and ⊥\bot otherwise; it is determined by π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}. We consider three events:

  • •

    E1E_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}: (w∗,z∗)=⊥(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})=\bot and b=1b=1;

  • •

    E2E_{\scriptscriptstyle 2}: (w∗,z∗)≠⊥(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})\neq\bot and ζ∉{(w∗,z∗)|ℐ,⊥}\zeta\notin\{(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}},\bot\};

  • •

    E3E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3}: (w∗,z∗)≠⊥(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})\neq\bot, ζ=(w∗,z∗)|ℐ\zeta=(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}}, and O⁡(𝗊𝗋𝗒~k)=𝖺𝗇𝗌~kO(\widetilde{\mathsf{qry}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k})=\widetilde{\mathsf{ans}}_{\scriptscriptstyle k} for every k∈[t]k\in[t].

If 𝒱\mathcal{V} accepts, then b=1b=1, ζ≠⊥\zeta\neq\bot, and every oracle check passes, so one of E1E_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}, E2E_{\scriptscriptstyle 2}, E3E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3} occurs. Suppose toward a contradiction that

Pr[⟨𝒫~,𝒱⟩(𝕩)=1]>13.\mathrm{Pr}\left[\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{P}},\mathcal{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]>\frac{1}{3}.

Then, by the union bound, Pr⁡[E1]>1/12\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}\right]>1/12, Pr⁡[E2]>1/12\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 2}\right]>1/12, or Pr⁡[E3]>1/6\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3}\right]>1/6, and we show that each case is impossible.

  • •

    Suppose Pr⁡[E1]>1/12\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}\right]>1/12. Let 𝒫~ew\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}} be the cheating prover for the encoded-witness IOP (𝒫ew,𝒱ew)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}},\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}}) that runs 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}} in the IOP step and then stops; the first message and the decision bit in this run are distributed as π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} and bb in our protocol. When (w∗,z∗)=⊥(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})=\bot, the first message π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} is δ\delta-far from 𝒞𝕩\mathcal{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbbm{x}}, the set of encodings of valid witnesses of R𝖢𝖲𝖠𝖳R_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CSAT}} for (⟨C⟩,x,a)(\langle C\rangle,x,a), because it is δ\delta-close to the encoding of at most one string and that string is not a valid witness. Therefore

    Pr⁡[b=1∧Δ⁡(π1,𝒞𝕩)>δ|(π1,b)←⟨𝒫~ew,𝒱ew⟩​(⟨C⟩,x,a)]≥Pr⁡[E1]>112≥ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯​(δ),\mathrm{Pr}\left[b=1\;\land\;\Delta(\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\mathcal{C}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbbm{x}})>\delta\;\middle|\;(\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},b)\leftarrow\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}},\mathcal{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{ew}}\rangle(\langle C\rangle,x,a)\right]\geq\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}\right]>\frac{1}{12}\geq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}(\delta),

    contradicting the soundness of Lemma 3.36 (Definition 3.34).

  • •

    Suppose Pr⁡[E2]>1/12\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 2}\right]>1/12. By averaging, there is a transcript of the IOP step together with a choice of the sampled gates, which fix π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}, (w∗,z∗)≠⊥(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})\neq\bot, and ℐ\mathcal{I}, conditioned on which E2E_{\scriptscriptstyle 2} occurs with probability greater than 1/121/12. Let 𝒫~dec\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}} be the cheating prover for the decoder (𝒫dec,𝐃)(\mathcal{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},\mathbf{D}) that has this transcript and these gates hardwired and continues to run 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}} from the decoding step; the output of 𝐃\mathbf{D} in this run is distributed as ζ\zeta in our protocol under the same conditioning. Since π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} is δ\delta-close to 𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(w∗,z∗)\mathsf{Enc}(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*}), we get

    Pr⁡[ζ∉{(w∗,z∗)|ℐ,⊥}|ζ←⟨𝒫~dec,𝐃π1⟩​(ℐ)]>112≥ϵdec​(δ,|ℐ|),\mathrm{Pr}\left[\zeta\notin\{(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})|_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{I}},\bot\}\;\middle|\;\zeta\leftarrow\langle\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{dec}},\mathbf{D}^{\scriptscriptstyle\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}}\rangle(\mathcal{I})\right]>\frac{1}{12}\geq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathrm{dec}}}(\delta,|\mathcal{I}|),

    contradicting the decoding error of Lemma 3.31 (Definition 3.30).

  • •

    Suppose Pr⁡[E3]>1/6\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3}\right]>1/6. When (w∗,z∗)≠⊥(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*})\neq\bot, it is a valid witness, so C⁡(x,w∗)=a≠CO​(x)C(x,w^{\scriptscriptstyle*})=a\neq C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x), and by robustness (Definition 3.14) O⁡(𝗊𝗋𝗒j​(w∗))≠wj∗O(\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle j}(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*}))\neq w^{\scriptscriptstyle*}_{\scriptscriptstyle j} for more than ε​𝗊C\varepsilon\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} indices j∈[𝗊C]j\in[\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}], with 𝗊𝗋𝗒j​(⋅)\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle j}(\cdot) as in that definition. On E3E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3} the decoded bits are those of (w∗,z∗)(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*}), so the kk-th decoded pair is (𝗊𝗋𝗒jk​(w∗),wjk∗)(\mathsf{qry}_{\scriptscriptstyle j_{\scriptscriptstyle k}}(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*}),w^{\scriptscriptstyle*}_{\scriptscriptstyle j_{\scriptscriptstyle k}}), and every oracle check passes only if no sampled gate is one of these indices. The sampled set is uniformly random and independent of (w∗,z∗)(w^{\scriptscriptstyle*},z^{\scriptscriptstyle*}), which is determined by π1\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}, sent before the sampling. Hence Pr⁡[E3]≤(1−ε)t≤e−ε​t≤1/6\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3}\right]\leq(1-\varepsilon)^{\scriptscriptstyle t}\leq e^{\scriptscriptstyle-\varepsilon t}\leq 1/6 if t=⌈(ln⁡6)/ε⌉t=\lceil(\ln 6)/\varepsilon\rceil, and Pr⁡[E3]=0\mathrm{Pr}\left[E_{\scriptscriptstyle 3}\right]=0 if t=𝗊Ct=\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}, a contradiction.

Hence 𝒱\mathcal{V} accepts with probability at most 1/31/3. If 𝗊C=0\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}=0, then C⁡(x)=CO​(x)≠aC(x)=C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)\neq a, so there is no valid witness and only E1E_{\scriptscriptstyle 1} can occur.

Efficiency.

The circuit CC has 𝗊C≤S\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}\leq S private input bits and S−𝗊CS-\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} gates, so Lemma 3.36 applies to it with N′=S+n+mN^{\prime}=S+n+m as in the statement of the theorem, and the list ℐ\mathcal{I} has at most t⋅wO≤⌈(ln⁡6)/ε⌉⋅wO=O~​(1/ε)t\cdot w_{\scriptscriptstyle O}\leq\lceil(\ln 6)/\varepsilon\rceil\cdot w_{\scriptscriptstyle O}=\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon) positions, where wOw_{\scriptscriptstyle O} is one plus the maximum fan-in of an oracle gate, which is polylogarithmic by hypothesis. The round complexity, proof query complexity, proof length, and prover time are the sums of those of the IOP in Lemma 3.36 and of the decoder in Lemma 3.31; in particular the prover time is O⁡(N′)+O⁡(|ℐ|)=O⁡(N′)+O~​(1/ε)O(N^{\prime})+O(|\mathcal{I}|)=O(N^{\prime})+\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon). The the verifier preprocessing time is that of the encoded-witness IOP plus the time O~​(S)\widetilde{O}(S) to compute ⟨C⟩\langle C\rangle and the positions from ⟨CO⟩\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle. The verifier makes t=O⁡(1/ε)t=O(1/\varepsilon) oracle queries, and its online time is that of the IOP plus that of the decoder plus O~​(|ℐ|)\widetilde{O}(|\mathcal{I}|) to read the positions and form the queries, for a total of O~​(n+m+1/ε)\widetilde{O}(n+m+1/\varepsilon).

5 Relativizing Rewindable Interactive Proofs

In this section we formally define relativizing rewindable interactive proofs (Section 5.1), show how to turn any relativizing IOP into a relativizing RIP (Section 5.2), and define the efficiency that we aim for and prove our main theorem (Section 5.3); in Section A.1 we show that RIPs are as powerful as MIPs.

5.1 Definition

As mentioned in Section 1, when the prover is an AI model, the verifier can save a snapshot of the model’s state and later restore it. We capture this by letting the verifier query the prover on any history of its choice. Since the prover may be assumed deterministic (Remark 5.6), it is determined by its next-message function, which maps the common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x} and a sequence (ρ1,…,ρj)(\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j}) of verifier messages to the prover’s reply after receiving these messages in this order; querying it on a history is the same as restoring the snapshot taken after that history and sending the last message.

Definition 5.1 (Rewindable interactive proof).

A rewindable interactive proof (RIP) for a relation RR is a pair (𝐏,𝐕)(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{V}) of a deterministic prover, given by its next-message function 𝐏⁡(𝕩,⋅)\mathbf{P}(\mathbbm{x},\cdot), and a probabilistic polynomial-time verifier 𝐕\mathbf{V} with oracle access to 𝐏⁡(𝕩,⋅)\mathbf{P}(\mathbbm{x},\cdot), which it may query adaptively on any sequence of messages. The parties receive a common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, and the honest prover additionally receives a witness 𝕨\mathbbm{w} with (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R. At the end, the verifier accepts or rejects.

The protocol satisfies the completeness and soundness properties defined below.

We write 𝐕𝐏⁡(𝕩,⋅)​(𝕩)=1\mathbf{V}^{\mathbf{P}(\mathbbm{x},\cdot)}(\mathbbm{x})=1 when the verifier accepts after interacting with the prover on common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x}. The probabilities below are over the verifier’s random bits.

Definition 5.2 (Completeness).

An RIP for RR has perfect completeness if, for every (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R, the honest prover satisfies

Pr[𝐕𝐏(𝕩,𝕨,⋅)(𝕩)=1]=1.\mathrm{Pr}\left[\mathbf{V}^{\mathbf{P}(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w},\cdot)}(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]=1.
Definition 5.3 (Soundness).

An RIP for RR has soundness error ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}} if, for every 𝕩∉ℒ\mathbbm{x}\notin\mathcal{L} and every function 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}} from sequences of messages to replies,

Pr[𝐕𝐏~(𝕩)=1]≤ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯(|𝕩|).\mathrm{Pr}\left[\mathbf{V}^{\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}}(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}}(|\mathbbm{x}|).
Definition 5.4 (Relativizing RIP).

Fix an oracle OO and a relativized relation ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} as in Definition 3.5. A relativizing RIP for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is an RIP for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} in which the verifier and the prover, including a cheating prover, have black-box access to the same oracle OO. The protocol relativizes if its completeness, soundness, and efficiency guarantees hold for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} for every oracle OO.

Remark 5.5 (Preprocessing).

As in Remark 3.22, an RIP with preprocessing for instances of the form 𝕩=(𝕩pre,𝕩post)\mathbbm{x}=(\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}},\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}) has a verifier that is a pair 𝐕=(𝐕pre,𝐕post)\mathbf{V}=(\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}},\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}). First 𝐕pre\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} receives 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} and outputs a state 𝗌𝗍𝐕\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}}. Then 𝐕post\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} receives 𝗌𝗍𝐕\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}} and 𝕩post\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} and queries the prover. Completeness and soundness are as in Definitions 5.2 and 5.3.

Remark 5.6 (Deterministic prover).

Assuming a deterministic prover loses no generality. For completeness, the honest prover’s random tape can be fixed and included in its state. For soundness, a randomized cheating prover is a distribution over deterministic next-message functions, so its acceptance probability is at most that of the best of them, provided that a snapshot includes the prover’s random tape.

We consider the following efficiency parameters of a (relativizing preprocessing) RIP, where each query to 𝐏⁡(𝕩,⋅)\mathbf{P}(\mathbbm{x},\cdot) counts as one message from the verifier and one from the prover:

  • •
