    Round complexity 𝗋𝖱𝖨𝖯\mathsf{r}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{RIP}}: the number of back-and-forth rounds between the verifier and the prover. Queries made in parallel count as one round.

  • •

    Prover query complexity 𝗊𝐏\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}}: the number of verifier queries to 𝐏⁡(𝕩,⋅)\mathbf{P}(\mathbbm{x},\cdot).

  • •

    Communication complexity 𝖼𝖼\mathsf{cc}: the total number of bits in the verifier’s queries and the prover’s answers.

  • •

    Verifier oracle query complexity 𝗊O\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle O}: the number of verifier calls to an external oracle OO, when present.

  • •

    Verifier preprocessing time t𝐕pret_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}}}: for an RIP with preprocessing (Remark 5.5), the running time of 𝐕pre\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}}, which bounds |𝗌𝗍𝐕||\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}}|.

  • •

    Verifier online time t𝐕t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}}: the running time of 𝐕post\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}, with random access to 𝗌𝗍𝐕\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}}.

  • •

    Prover running time t𝐏t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}}: the honest prover’s total time to answer all queries.

Saving and restoring a snapshot is not charged; the number of restores is at most the prover query complexity.

5.2 From IOPs to RIPs

The compilation is inspired by the standard one from an IOP to a two-prover protocol [12, 42], as applied to IOPs in [15, Appendix A], in which one prover answers the verifier’s proof queries and a second, non-communicating prover answers one of them at random to bind the first to fixed proof strings, at the cost of dividing the rejection probability by the query count. With a rewindable prover the verifier binds the prover itself: it obtains each symbol of a proof string by restoring the prover to its state when that string was fixed, so the prover cannot answer adaptively and the compilation loses nothing in soundness.

Lemma 5.7 (IOP-to-RIP transformation).

Let (𝒫,𝒱)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{V}) be a relativizing IOP (Definition 3.21) for a relativized relation ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} with perfect completeness, soundness error ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}, round complexity 𝗋𝖨𝖮𝖯\mathsf{r}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{IOP}}, and proof query complexity 𝗊π\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\pi}. Then (𝒫,𝒱)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{V}) can be transformed into a relativizing rewindable interactive proof (𝐏,𝐕)(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{V}) (Definition 5.4) for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} with the following properties.

  • •

    Perfect completeness.

  • •

    Soundness error: at most ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}.

  • •

    Round complexity: O⁡(𝗋𝖨𝖮𝖯+𝗊π)O(\mathsf{r}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{IOP}}+\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\pi}).

  • •

    Verifier oracle query complexity: the same as that of 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

If (𝒫,𝒱)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{V}) has preprocessing (Remark 3.22), then so does (𝐏,𝐕)(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{V}) (Remark 5.5), with the same verifier preprocessing. The verifier 𝐕\mathbf{V} runs 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and the honest prover runs 𝒫\mathcal{P} once, with additional work only to process the query addresses and replies.

Proof.

The protocol.

The parties receive 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, and the honest prover also receives 𝕨\mathbbm{w}. Query addresses are tagged so that a history ending in a query is distinguishable from one ending in a verifier message.

  • •

    Prover 𝐏\mathbf{P}: runs 𝒫\mathcal{P} on (𝕩,𝕨)(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w}). On receiving a verifier message ρ\rho, it forwards ρ\rho to 𝒫\mathcal{P}, which computes its next proof string, and replies with the empty message. On receiving a query qq after j−1j-1 verifier messages, it replies with the symbol πj​(q)\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle j}(q) of the jj-th proof string.

  • •

    Verifier 𝐕\mathbf{V}: runs 𝒱\mathcal{V} on 𝕩\mathbbm{x} and makes 𝒱\mathcal{V}’s oracle queries to OO itself. Whenever 𝒱\mathcal{V} wishes to read position qq of the jj-th proof string, 𝐕\mathbf{V} queries 𝐏\mathbf{P} on the history (ρ1,…,ρj−1,q)(\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j-1},q), where ρ1,…,ρj−1\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j-1} are the messages that 𝒱\mathcal{V} sent before the jj-th proof string, and hands the reply to 𝒱\mathcal{V} as that symbol. Queries that 𝒱\mathcal{V} makes at the same time are made in parallel, and a message that 𝒱\mathcal{V} reads in full is obtained by querying all of its positions. 𝐕\mathbf{V} accepts if and only if 𝒱\mathcal{V} accepts.

In the snapshot view of Definition 5.1, querying 𝐏\mathbf{P} on (ρ1,…,ρj−1,q)(\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j-1},q) restores the prover to its state just after it fixed the jj-th proof string and asks for one symbol of it, which is why the prover cannot answer adaptively.

Completeness.

The honest prover’s replies are the symbols of 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s proof strings, so the simulated 𝒱\mathcal{V} sees exactly the honest IOP interaction and accepts with probability 11.

Soundness.

Consider an instance 𝕩∉ℒRO\mathbbm{x}\notin\mathcal{L}_{\scriptscriptstyle R^{\scriptscriptstyle O}} and a cheating prover 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}, which we may assume to be deterministic (Remark 5.6). Define a cheating IOP prover 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}} that, having received the verifier messages ρ1,…,ρj−1\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j-1}, sends the proof string

sj​(q)≔𝐏~​(ρ1,…,ρj−1,q).s_{\scriptscriptstyle j}(q)\coloneq\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}(\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j-1},q).

This is a valid IOP prover strategy, since sjs_{\scriptscriptstyle j} depends only on messages available when string jj is sent. Every symbol that 𝐕\mathbf{V} obtains from 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}} is the corresponding symbol of sjs_{\scriptscriptstyle j}, so the view of the simulated 𝒱\mathcal{V} against 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}} is exactly its view against 𝒫~\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}, and 𝐕\mathbf{V} accepts with probability at most ϵ𝖨𝖮𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{IOP}}}.

Efficiency.

The simulation uses the rounds of the IOP, with the queries of each round made in parallel, plus at most one round per query for queries that 𝒱\mathcal{V} makes adaptively, for O⁡(𝗋𝖨𝖮𝖯+𝗊π)O(\mathsf{r}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{IOP}}+\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\pi}) rounds in total. The verifier’s oracle queries are those of 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The verifier’s work beyond 𝒱\mathcal{V}’s is to form the query addresses and copy the message prefixes, and the honest prover’s work beyond 𝒫\mathcal{P}’s is to restore snapshots and read symbols. Preprocessing is preserved since 𝐕\mathbf{V} preprocesses exactly as 𝒱\mathcal{V} does, and the argument applies verbatim when all parties have access to an oracle OO.

∎

5.3 RIPs with linear-time provers and succinct verifiers

In our setting, the honest prover should take not much more time than evaluating the circuit, and the verifier should do substantially less work than evaluating the circuit itself. To verify the evaluation of an oracle circuit COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O}, we use an RIP with preprocessing for the relation R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O} of Definition 3.16: the parties receive the instance 𝕩=(⟨CO⟩,x,a)\mathbbm{x}=(\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle,x,a), where 𝕩pre=⟨CO⟩\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}}=\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle and 𝕩post=(x,a)\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}=(x,a), the honest prover receives the transcript zz, and the claim is that CO​(x)=aC^{\scriptscriptstyle O}(x)=a. We now prove our main theorem by applying the transformation of Section 5.2 to the relativizing IOP of Section 4.

Theorem 5.8.

Fix O:{0,1}∗→{0,1}O:\{0,1\}^{\scriptscriptstyle*}\to\{0,1\} and 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1, and let COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} be an oracle circuit with an input of length nn, an output of length mm, and SS gates, and let N′≔S+n+mN^{\prime}\coloneq S+n+m as in Theorem 4.1. Suppose that the oracle queries of COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} have length polylogarithmic in N′N^{\prime}. For every σ≥1\sigma\geq 1, R𝖢𝖵𝖠𝖫OR_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{CVAL}}^{\scriptscriptstyle O}, for instances (⟨CO⟩,x,a)(\langle C^{\scriptscriptstyle O}\rangle,x,a) with this circuit such that COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is ε\varepsilon-robust with respect to xx, has a relativizing rewindable interactive proof with preprocessing (Remark 5.5) with the following properties, where O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot) hides factors polylogarithmic in N′N^{\prime} and running times count field operations.

  • •

    Perfect completeness.

  • •

    Soundness error: at most 2−σ2^{\scriptscriptstyle-\sigma}.

  • •

    Round complexity: O⁡(σ​log⁡N′)O(\sigma\log N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Communication complexity: O~​(σ/ε)\widetilde{O}(\sigma/\varepsilon) field elements.

  • •

    Verifier oracle query complexity: O⁡(σ​min⁡{𝗊C,1/ε})O(\sigma\min\{\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C},1/\varepsilon\}).

  • •

    Verifier preprocessing time: O~​(N′)\widetilde{O}(N^{\prime}).

  • •

    Verifier online time: O~​(σ​(n+m+1/ε))\widetilde{O}(\sigma(n+m+1/\varepsilon)).

  • •

    Prover time: O⁡(σ​N′)+O~​(σ/ε)O(\sigma N^{\prime})+\widetilde{O}(\sigma/\varepsilon).

In particular, for constant σ\sigma and 1/ε≤logO⁡(1)⁡N′1/\varepsilon\leq\log^{\scriptscriptstyle O(1)}N^{\prime}, the prover runs in time O⁡(N′)O(N^{\prime}), linear in the size of the computation, and the verifier’s online time is O~​(n+m)\widetilde{O}(n+m); the number of oracle queries, O⁡(min⁡{𝗊C,1/ε})O(\min\{\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C},1/\varepsilon\}), is sublinear in 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} whenever ε​𝗊C\varepsilon\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} grows without bound.

The proof applies the transformation of Lemma 5.7 to the IOP of Theorem 4.1 and reduces the soundness error to 2−σ2^{-\sigma} by sequential repetition, restoring the prover to its initial state before each run. We then remark on computing proof strings on demand (Remark 5.9).

Proof.

Apply Lemma 5.7 to the IOP of Theorem 4.1. The result is a relativizing rewindable interactive proof with preprocessing with soundness error at most 1/31/3, O⁡(log⁡N′)O(\log N^{\prime}) rounds, O⁡(min⁡{𝗊C,1/ε})O(\min\{\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C},1/\varepsilon\}) verifier oracle queries, communication O~​(1/ε)\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon), verifier online time O~​(n+m+1/ε)\widetilde{O}(n+m+1/\varepsilon), verifier preprocessing time O~​(N′)\widetilde{O}(N^{\prime}), and prover time O⁡(N′)+O~​(1/ε)O(N^{\prime})+\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon). The verifier runs it R≔⌈σ/log2⁡3⌉R\coloneq\lceil\sigma/\log_{2}3\rceil times sequentially with fresh randomness, restoring the prover to its initial state before each run, and accepts if and only if every run accepts. Perfect completeness is preserved. For soundness, fix a false instance and a deterministic cheating prover 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}. Since each run queries 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}} only on histories of that run, the runs are independent executions of the protocol against the same prover, each accepted with probability at most 1/31/3, so all are accepted with probability at most 3−R≤2−σ3^{\scriptscriptstyle-R}\leq 2^{\scriptscriptstyle-\sigma}. The round complexity, communication, oracle queries, online time, and prover time are RR times those of one run, and the preprocessing is done once, which gives the stated parameters. ∎

Remark 5.9 (Computing proof strings on demand).

Bitansky and Chiesa [17] observed that the provers of a multi-prover interactive proof [12] (Appendix A) need not store a proof: each only ever returns single symbols of proof strings, so it can compute each symbol when it is queried. Holmgren and Rothblum [50] sharpened this to provers with time O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(T) and space S+o⁡(S)S+o(S) for RAM computations. The same ability to compute symbols on demand is available to a rewindable prover, which also only returns single symbols: its state at the posting of a string already determines the answer at every position, and restoring that state before each query keeps the answer from depending on anything later, so the honest prover can fix a proof string without computing or storing it in full. This is an advantage over hash-based SNARGs: in a Merkle-based compilation of an IOP into a SNARG such as Flock’s [27], the prover must compute every proof string in full in order to hash it. Computing on demand can be used to save prover time or prover space:

  • •

    Prover time. Most known linear-time provers come from tensor and interleaved codes of linear-time encodable codes [18, 58, 20, 19, 66, 47, 21, 25], as does the prover of Theorem 5.8, which specifically uses TensorSwitch [25] (Lemma 3.31). The concretely fastest IOPs, including Flock’s, which our implementation builds on (Section 6), encode with Reed–Solomon codes instead, whose encoding relies on the fast Fourier transform (FFT) and makes their provers quasi-linear; the linear-time instantiation is at present a theoretical result. Computing on demand avoids part of the FFT: our compilation of Flock’s IOP applies only the first layers of the FFT to every row when it posts a proof string and finishes the remaining layers of a row only when the verifier asks for it. Together with the removal of the hash function and the smaller security parameter, this accounts for the speedup of our prover over Flock’s SNARG prover in Section 6.3.

  • •

    Prover space. Theorem 5.8 bounds the prover’s time but not its space, and as described the honest prover stores the encoding 𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(u)\mathsf{Enc}(u) of its witness, which takes space O~​(N′)\widetilde{O}(N^{\prime}). Suppose that COC^{\scriptscriptstyle O} computes the TT-step execution of an oracle machine that uses space SS, so that N′=O~​(T)N^{\prime}=\widetilde{O}(T) and the prover can regenerate uu in space O⁡(S)O(S) by running the machine again. Then, for the Reed–Solomon instantiation, each message of the prover can be computed in one pass over the regenerated uu, as in the streaming prover of Cormode, Mitzenmacher, and Thaler [39], so the prover runs in space O~​(S+1/ε)\widetilde{O}(S+1/\varepsilon) and in time O~​(σ​T)\widetilde{O}(\sigma T), at the price of running the machine, and hence querying OO, once per round. The verifier is unchanged. We do not work out the details here.

6 Implementation and Experiments

As a proof of concept, we implement our protocol and evaluate it on an MNIST task inspired by the AI debate experiment of Irving, Christiano, and Amodei [51]. Briefly, in their experiment, there are two provers, or agents, and a judge which is trained to classify an MNIST image from a few nonzero pixels. A random MNIST image is shown to the agents but not to the judge. One agent claims the correct label and the other agent claims an incorrect label, e.g., the image contains a 5, and one claims 5 and the other claims 6. They take turns revealing a nonzero pixel in the image to the judge until four or six pixels are revealed. Then the judge chooses which agent wins based on which of their labels has the higher logit. Their experiment studies how often an honest agent wins against a dishonest one; we instead measure the cost of verifying a robust computation that uses their judge as its oracle.

Following their experiment, we train a sparse MNIST classifier using the same architecture; it correctly classifies 59.4%59.4\% of random six-pixel views. We use its predictions to define an oracle: given a sparse view and a candidate digit yy, the oracle outputs 11 if the classifier predicts yy and 00 otherwise. Our circuits query this oracle on many sparse views of an image and output whether a majority of the views vote for the candidate digit. We vary the number of sparse views to study how the cost of verification scales with the size of the circuit. We also compile an existing IOP for a standard, oracle-free computation, Flock’s IOP for BLAKE3 [27], into an RIP and compare it with Flock’s own SNARG (Section 6.3).

6.1 Implementation

Our implementation is open source22 2 https://github.com/ZiyiGuan/oversight-rip and written in Rust. It follows the construction of Section 5, building the encoded-witness IOP of Section 3.4 from components of Binius [40], Flock [27], and Ligero [3], and compiling it into an RIP as in Lemma 5.7: the prover keeps each proof string it computes instead of sending it, and the verifier reads a symbol of a proof string by restoring the prover to its state at the moment that string was fixed and asking for that symbol, so that no answer can depend on anything the verifier sent later. The proof strings are opened in the layout of Ligero [3]: the encoded witness is arranged in rows of about N\sqrt{N} entries and the verifier reads 6464 whole columns, which gives a proximity error below 2−422^{-42}. Together with tt sampled oracle gates, the smallest number with (1−ε)t≤2−41(1-\varepsilon)^{t}\leq 2^{-41} for the circuit’s robustness parameter ε\varepsilon, a single execution of the protocol has soundness error at most 2−40.532^{-40.53} at every circuit size, against computationally unbounded provers; there are no repetitions.

The majority circuit sums the oracle answers in a tree whose levels consist of identical blocks, so the verifier’s work for a level is that of one block and this circuit family needs no preprocessing; for a general circuit, the preprocessing of Remark 5.5 would take its place. The classifier’s answers are computed in advance, so both the protocol and direct evaluation of the circuit query the oracle by table lookup. All timings are from AWS Graviton4 instances, one single-threaded process per core, with transparent huge pages enabled. Absolute times are specific to that core; every ratio below is between measurements on the same core type.

6.2 MNIST experiments

Concretely, call an MNIST image with six nonzero pixels revealed a view. For each circuit, we fix an MNIST image together with qCq_{C} randomly sampled views of the image; the image and views are hardwired into the description of the circuit. On input a candidate digit yy, the circuit queries the oracle on each of its qCq_{C} views and outputs 11 if more than half of the views vote for yy. We can compute the robustness parameters for these circuits exactly: for each digit yy, we compute the minimum number of oracle answers that would need to be changed in order to flip the output of the circuit on yy. Let mm be the minimum of this quantity over all ten digits. Then changing at most m−1m-1 oracle answers cannot change the output of the circuit on any input, so the circuit is (m−1)/𝗊C(m-1)/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}-robust with respect to every input.

To choose instances to run our circuit on, we scan the MNIST test set in order. For each image, we sample 282^{8} random views and construct the corresponding circuit. We select the first 50 images for which this circuit accepts the correct digit and has robustness parameter at least 1/81/8. We use these same 50 images throughout the experiment, and consider

𝗊C∈{28,210,212,…,226},\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}\in\{2^{8},2^{10},2^{12},\ldots,2^{26}\},

sampling additional views of each image as 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} increases (one image has fewer than 2242^{24} distinct six-pixel views and three have fewer than 2262^{26}; those images are omitted at those sizes). For each image and circuit size, we recompute the robustness parameter and run the complete protocol once, at soundness error 2−402^{-40}. The median robustness parameter remains between 0.300.30 and 0.320.32 at every circuit size.

All runs with the honest provers accepted, as expected from perfect completeness. Table 1 reports detailed costs, and Fig. 1 shows how the verifier scales relative to direct evaluation. All values are medians over the images.

Since the robustness parameter remains nearly constant, the median number of oracle queries made by the verifier stays between 7474 and 8080 as 𝗊C\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C} grows from 282^{8} to 2262^{26}. At 2262^{26} views, the verifier makes 840,000×840{,}000\times fewer oracle queries than the circuit. The verifier’s online time also grows much more slowly than direct evaluation: it grows from 0.450.45 ms to 1.91.9 ms, while direct evaluation grows from 0.06​μ0.06\,\mus to 1616 ms. Because direct evaluation costs only about 0.230.23 ns per view, the two cross between 2222^{22} and 2242^{24} views, and at 2262^{26} the verifier takes 0.12×0.12\times as long as direct evaluation. This baseline is pessimistic for the protocol: both direct evaluation and the protocol answer oracle queries by table lookup, whereas in the intended setting each query is a model evaluation and dominates everything else. With a costly oracle, direct evaluation pays qCq_{C} evaluations while the verifier pays his 7474 to 8080, so the crossing would come at a far smaller circuit, and the prover’s overhead over direct evaluation would shrink toward the cost of its field arithmetic alone; the oracle-query counts in Table 1 are the measure that transfers.

At small qCq_{C}, the verifier is slower than direct evaluation because protocol overhead dominates: the verifier performs the IOP interaction and opening checks, whereas direct evaluation requires only qCq_{C} table lookups. As qCq_{C} grows, direct evaluation grows linearly, while the verifier’s time grows by a factor of 1.11.1 to 1.31.3 per fourfold increase in qCq_{C}, so their ratio falls by a factor of 3.03.0 to 3.73.7 per step. The verifier time grows because our implementation uses the Ligero layout [3], whose openings have size about N\sqrt{N}, rather than the polylogarithmic cost in Theorem 5.8.

The prover cost settles at a constant multiple of direct evaluation from 𝗊C=220\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}=2^{20} on: the prover, which generates the witness and makes all qCq_{C} oracle lookups, takes about 60×60\times direct evaluation (0.90.9 s at 2262^{26} views); at the small sizes it is dominated by fixed costs.

6.3 Comparison with a SNARG

In Section 1 we argued that rewinding brings efficiency gains over a SNARG. The relativizing protocols of Chen, Kalai, and Xi [30] offer no comparison, since they have no implementation and their prover is only polynomial-time, so we compare prover time against the best known concretely efficient proof system for ordinary, oracle-free computations, Flock [27], whose IOP proves batches of BLAKE3 compressions and whose SNARG, a succinct non-interactive argument, compiles it with Merkle commitments. A SNARG is how an IOP is made practical in the applications of proof systems to date, where the verifier has no control over the prover’s machine and so cannot rewind it: the IOP’s proof strings are committed to with a hash function and the interaction is removed. Rewinding is another way to make the same IOP practical, so comparing our compilation with Flock’s SNARG measures what each way costs. We compiled Flock’s IOP into an RIP, keeping its proof strings, queries, and checks: the prover runs Flock’s prover with the Merkle commitments removed, and the verifier rewinds it to its state at each proof string’s posting before every row query, as in the compilation of Lemma 5.7, so that its answers depend on the posting alone; the verifier runs Flock’s verifier on those rows. A false statement is then accepted with at most the IOP’s own error (Lemma 5.7).

The RIP gains in three ways over the SNARG. It needs no hash function, since rewinding replaces the Merkle commitment. Nor does it need to encode every proof string in full, since nothing is hashed: the prover applies only the first layers of the FFT when it posts a string and finishes a row only when it is queried (Remark 5.9). And it needs far fewer bits of security: a SNARG prover can retry offline until the hash-derived challenges are favorable, so Flock’s default configuration targets a 128128-bit per-round work factor, whereas a cheating prover in the RIP gets one attempt per execution, which the verifier observes, so 4040 bits suffice. We therefore run Flock’s IOP at its 4040-bit interactive parameter setting and, since a smaller field suffices as well, over a 6464-bit base field with a 128128-bit extension for the challenges, which Flock’s release does not offer and which halves the field arithmetic. The error is 2−42.42^{-42.4} to 2−42.92^{-42.9} at these sizes, assuming that the IOP’s query and algebraic error terms compose statistically, as Flock’s parameter code assumes.

Table 2 reports prover times at 2222^{22} to 2342^{34} witness bits (282^{8} to 2202^{20} compressions) on one Graviton 4 core, medians of three executions. Our prover is 1.81.8 to 2.1×2.1\times faster than Flock’s SNARG prover at every size.

6.4 Limitations

Our experiments are intended as a proof of concept rather than as a realistic scalable-oversight benchmark. The circuits are simple majority circuits over random sparse views, and the 50 images are selected so that their 𝗊C=28\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle C}=2^{8} circuits have robustness parameter at least 1/81/8; thus, the experiments do not show that arbitrary MNIST instances or more complex oracle computations satisfy our robustness assumption. Moreover, unlike in the MNIST debate experiment, the sparse views are sampled randomly instead of chosen adversarially (by debating agents). The majority is also a statistical quantity: for a majority over hardwired views, the verifier could estimate the output himself by sampling about as many views as he queries in the protocol, with no prover at all. The protocol is needed for circuits that process the oracle answers further or choose later queries from earlier answers; our circuits do neither.

Because the image and views are hardwired into the circuit, each image and circuit size is its own instance; the verifier needs no preprocessing here only because the majority circuit’s levels consist of identical blocks, and a general circuit would need the preprocessing of Remark 5.5, with its own amortization question. The verifier’s time grows with the square root of the trace, from the Ligero layout of the opening, rather than polylogarithmically as in Theorem 5.8. Even though the verifier becomes cheaper than direct evaluation on the largest circuits, the prover cost remains a constant factor over direct evaluation, about 60×60\times at the largest sizes, where direct evaluation is qCq_{C} table lookups and the prover performs field arithmetic over the entire encoded witness; on the BLAKE3 instances, where there is no such gap to begin with, our prover is cheaper than the SNARG’s. The protocol also treats saving and restoring the prover’s state as free; for a real model each restore copies its state, and in both compilations the prover is restored before every query.

Appendix A Multi-prover interactive proofs

Rewindable interactive proofs are closely related to multi-prover interactive proofs (MIPs) [12]: a restored snapshot gives the verifier an interaction that the prover cannot connect to any other, much as a second non-communicating prover would. MIPs are in turn equivalent in power to probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) [41, 7, 6], since two non-communicating provers can simulate a proof string, at a loss in soundness, and a proof string can hold the provers’ strategies [42]; we therefore present only the equivalence of MIPs and RIPs. This appendix recalls the definition of MIPs and shows that the two models have the same power (Section A.1): every MIP is an RIP with the same soundness error, and every RIP whose verifier makes 𝗊𝐏\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}} queries to the prover is a two-prover MIP with soundness error 1−(1−ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯)/𝗊𝐏1-(1-\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}})/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}}.

A multi-prover interactive proof lets several powerful provers try to convince a weak verifier that an instance has a valid witness.

Definition A.1 (Multi-prover interactive proof system).

A pp-prover interactive proof for a relation RR is an interactive protocol between a probabilistic polynomial-time verifier 𝐕\mathbf{V} and pp computationally unbounded provers 𝐏1,…,𝐏p\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle p}. The parties receive a common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, and the honest provers additionally receive a witness 𝕨\mathbbm{w} with (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R.

The provers may agree on a strategy beforehand but cannot communicate during the protocol: each prover’s messages depend only on 𝕩\mathbbm{x}, its agreed strategy, and its own interaction with the verifier. At the end of the interaction, the verifier accepts or rejects.

The protocol satisfies the completeness and soundness properties defined below.

We write ⟨𝐏1​(𝕨),…,𝐏p​(𝕨),𝐕⟩​(𝕩)=1\langle\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}(\mathbbm{w}),\ldots,\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle p}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathbf{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1 when the verifier accepts after interacting with the provers on common input 𝕩\mathbbm{x}. The probabilities below are over the verifier’s private random bits (we assume without loss of generality that the provers are deterministic).

Definition A.2 (Completeness).

An MIP for RR has perfect completeness if, for every (𝕩,𝕨)∈R(\mathbbm{x},\mathbbm{w})\in R, the honest provers satisfy

Pr[⟨𝐏1(𝕨),…,𝐏p(𝕨),𝐕⟩(𝕩)=1]=1.\mathrm{Pr}\left[\langle\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}(\mathbbm{w}),\ldots,\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle p}(\mathbbm{w}),\mathbf{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]=1.
Definition A.3 (Soundness).

An MIP for RR has soundness error ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}} if, for every 𝕩∉ℒ\mathbbm{x}\notin\mathcal{L} and every tuple of possibly computationally unbounded cheating provers 𝐏~1,…,𝐏~p\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle p},

Pr[⟨𝐏~1,…,𝐏~p,𝐕⟩(𝕩)=1]≤ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯(|𝕩|).\mathrm{Pr}\left[\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle p},\mathbf{V}\rangle(\mathbbm{x})=1\right]\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}}(|\mathbbm{x}|).
Definition A.4 (Relativizing MIP).

Fix an oracle OO and a relativized relation ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} as in Definition 3.5. A relativizing MIP for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} is an MIP for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} in which the verifier and all provers, including cheating provers, have black-box access to the same oracle OO. The protocol relativizes if its completeness, soundness, and efficiency guarantees hold for ROR^{\scriptscriptstyle O} for every oracle OO.

Remark A.5 (Preprocessing).

As in Remark 3.22, an MIP with preprocessing for instances of the form 𝕩=(𝕩pre,𝕩post)\mathbbm{x}=(\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}},\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}) has a verifier that is a pair 𝐕=(𝐕pre,𝐕post)\mathbf{V}=(\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}},\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}}). First 𝐕pre\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} receives 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} and outputs a state 𝗌𝗍𝐕\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}}. Then 𝐕post\mathbf{V}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} receives 𝗌𝗍𝐕\mathsf{st}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{V}} and 𝕩post\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{post}} and interacts with the provers. Completeness and soundness are as in Definitions A.2 and A.3.

Efficiency parameters are as for RIPs (Section 5.1), with parallel exchanges with different provers counting as one round and the prover running time taken as the sum over the honest provers.

A.1 Relation to RIPs

Rewindable interactive proofs are as powerful as MIPs: every MIP is a rewindable interactive proof with the same soundness error, and two provers can simulate a rewindable prover at a loss in the soundness error.

Lemma A.6 (MIP to RIP).

Every pp-prover interactive proof for RR with perfect completeness and soundness error ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}} yields a rewindable interactive proof for RR with perfect completeness and soundness error ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯=ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}}=\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}}, the same verifier complexity up to tagging each message with a prover index, and the same prover running time. If the MIP has preprocessing (Remark A.5), so does the RIP (Remark 5.5), with the same verifier preprocessing. The same holds for relativizing protocols.

Proof.

Let (𝐏1,…,𝐏p,𝐕)(\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle p},\mathbf{V}) be the MIP. The new verifier runs 𝐕\mathbf{V}, and whenever 𝐕\mathbf{V} has sent messages ρ1,…,ρj\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j} to prover ii, it obtains that prover’s reply by querying the rewindable prover on the history ((i,ρ1),…,(i,ρj))((i,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}),\ldots,(i,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j})). The honest rewindable prover answers a history tagged with ii as 𝐏i\mathbf{P}_{\scriptscriptstyle i} would, so completeness is preserved. For soundness, given any function 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}, define cheating MIP provers by 𝐏~i​(ρ1,…,ρj)≔𝐏~​((i,ρ1),…,(i,ρj))\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle i}(\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j})\coloneq\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}((i,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle 1}),\ldots,(i,\rho_{\scriptscriptstyle j})). Each 𝐏~i\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle i} depends only on its own history, so these are valid non-communicating MIP provers, and the new verifier’s view against 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}} is exactly that of 𝐕\mathbf{V} against 𝐏~1,…,𝐏~p\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle 1},\ldots,\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}_{\scriptscriptstyle p}. Hence the acceptance probability is at most ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}}, so ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯≤ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}}\leq\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}}. The new verifier preprocesses 𝕩pre\mathbbm{x}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{pre}} exactly as 𝐕\mathbf{V} does, and the same argument applies verbatim when all parties have access to an oracle OO.

∎

Lemma A.7 (RIP to MIP).

Every rewindable interactive proof for RR with perfect completeness and soundness error ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}} in which the verifier makes at most 𝗊𝐏\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}} queries to the prover yields a two-prover interactive proof for RR with perfect completeness and soundness error ϵ𝖬𝖨𝖯≤1−(1−ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯)/𝗊𝐏\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{MIP}}}\leq 1-(1-\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}})/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}}, with one additional round, in which the first prover answers the verifier’s queries and the second prover answers one query. The same holds for relativizing protocols and for protocols with preprocessing.

Proof.

The verifier runs the RIP, sending each query to the first prover, and at the end sends one of the queries, chosen uniformly at random, to the second prover and rejects if the two answers differ. With honest provers the answers always agree. For soundness, the second prover’s answers define a single next-message function, hence a cheating RIP prover 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}. Let CC be the event that the first prover’s answers agree with 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}} on every queried history. On CC the simulated RIP verifier’s view is its view against 𝐏~\widetilde{\mathbf{P}}, so Pr⁡[accept∧C]≤min⁡{ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯,Pr⁡[C]}\mathrm{Pr}\left[\text{accept}\wedge C\right]\leq\min\{\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}},\mathrm{Pr}\left[C\right]\}. Otherwise some answer disagrees, and the second prover’s query, chosen independently of the transcript, lands on it with probability at least 1/𝗊𝐏1/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}}, so Pr⁡[accept∧¬C]≤(1−1/𝗊𝐏)​Pr​[¬C]\mathrm{Pr}\left[\text{accept}\wedge\neg C\right]\leq(1-1/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}})\mathrm{Pr}\left[\neg C\right]. Writing b≔Pr⁡[¬C]b\coloneq\mathrm{Pr}\left[\neg C\right], the acceptance probability is at most min⁡{ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯,1−b}+b⁡(1−1/𝗊𝐏)≤1−(1−ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯)/𝗊𝐏\min\{\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}},1-b\}+b(1-1/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}})\leq 1-(1-\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}})/\mathsf{q}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{P}}, with the maximum at b=1−ϵ𝖱𝖨𝖯b=1-\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathsf{RIP}}}.
